utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall now continue to hear the closing arguments of the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Before I move on to General Pavkovic, there were two items I wanted to follow-up from yesterday. One regarded a question you addressed to Ms. Kravetz. You asked about whether it was our position to say that -- using the NATO bombing campaign as a cover on implementing the plan. You said, "Now, are you saying that's something which just happened because of a developing set of circumstances, or are you saying that they went to the peace negotiations with the plan in mind that, Well, when these break down NATO will bomb us and we'll use that as a cover for removing the population?" We take the position, Your Honour, that the accused's intention was to implement the plan to alter the ethnic composition in Kosovo. They took steps to ensure this including, we say, a step of not negotiating in good faith to achieve a peaceful solution. As it happened, the bombing did provide an opportunity to speed up the process and do it on a greater scale, but we say from October when you have that statement from Milosevic about, We'll have a solution in the spring, that there was the intention from that point on to remove a significant portion of the population in order to alter the ethnic balance to help ensure Serbian control of the province. If the bombing did not happen, we believe the accused still would have taken steps to implement the plan, but it's difficult to speculate about something that didn't happen. The fact is that bombing did occur, and we say that members of the JCE proceeded with the plan which had been conceived in October 1998. I hope that answers your question about our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two other things. In General Ojdanic's final brief, there are a couple of matters they raised that I just wanted to address. In paragraph 410, he asserts that the mens rea for forcible transfer requires an intent to permanently displace. We say that's not a correct statement of the law. For deportation, what is required is the forcible displacement of persons from an area in which they are lawfully present across a border without grounds permitted under international law. That's from the Stakic appeals judgement at paragraph 278. The Appeals Chamber held that no intent to displace permanently is required, nor is there a minimum threshold as far as the number of deportees. We refer you again to the Stakic appellate judgement at paragraph 307, the Brdjanin appellate judgement at paragraph 206, and regarding minimum numbers, Stakic at paragraph 320. And one other item. Between the time that we filed our briefs and today's arguments, there was a judgement in the Strugar case on the 17th of July that deals with an issue that you may address in reaching your final judgement, and that has to do with Article 7(3) and about whether a superior knew or had reason to know that his subordinate was about to commit crimes. I would like to direct your attention to paragraphs 301 and 304 of that judgement. Now, while a superior's knowledge -- paragraph 301 says, While a superior's knowledge and failure to punish his subordinate's past offences is insufficient in itself to conclude that the superior knew that future, similar -- that similar, future offences would be committed by the same group, this may, depending on the circumstances, nevertheless constitute sufficiently alarming information to justify further inquiry. And then in paragraph 4, they point out that the correct legal standard regarding the mens rea element under Article 7(3) is that "sufficiently alarming information putting a superior on notice of the risk, the risk, that crimes might subsequently be carried out by subordinates, and justifying further inquiry is sufficient to hold a superior liable under Article 7(3)." That's -- we think that's fairly new jurisprudence that the Court should be aware of in your deliberations on this matter. Now, there were other Defence arguments by the Ojdanic case -- Ojdanic Defence. One of them was the fair trial issue. Your Honour, that was raised on three earlier occasions by the Defence, and we say there's nothing new presented here to warrant a change your prior rulings on that. Now with that, I would like to turn to General Pavkovic, and General Pavkovic we know was the commander of the Pristina Corps in 1998 during the implementation of the plan to suppress terrorism and of the 3rd Army from January 1999. We say General Pavkovic contributed to the JCE, first of all, by arming non-Siptars; secondly, by breaching the October Agreement; and thirdly and most significantly, in planning, commanding, ordering, and coordinating VJ operations in controlled joint VJ and MUP combat actions. With regard to arming the non-Siptars, we spoke about this already when I was addressing General Ojdanic's role in that connection, and we looked at Exhibit P1415, which was the 26 June 1998 order from General Pavkovic, following on from an order from General Samardzic in the 3rd Army command providing for arming the non-Siptar population and organizing defence in those non-Siptar villages. So I won't go through that again. The other side of that coin was Pavkovic's involvement in disarming the Siptars, the Albanian population. Pavkovic reported about this in one of my favourite Exhibits, P2166, which we'll be talking about some more before I'm finished. That was the 29 October 1998 meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism. In that report he indicated that large quantities, over 150 tonnes of weapons and ammunition were confiscated and handed over in the course of implementing the plan; some 93 Siptar villages were disarmed; and as of the date of the report, he indicated at page 5 of that exhibit that 66 villages still needed to be disarmed. And we have evidence that that disarming programme in cooperation between the VJ and the MUP continued. You'll see in Exhibit P1197, which is a Joint Command operations report dated the 20th of November, 1998, that that work, that disarming programme, was ongoing. Next, we say General Pavkovic contributed to the JCE by breaching the October Agreement. It's set out in more detail in our closing brief, but in interviews after the war he, in my view, appeared to be bragging about the fact that they were able to bring in additional units into Kosovo during the time before the war practically under the nose of the OSCE verifiers. You can find that in Exhibits P1319 and P912. You've also heard evidence about that on several occasions in discussions of VJ collegium meetings. Some of those meetings include the 18th March 1999 meeting, which is found in Exhibit P938 at page 11, and also in the 10 December 1998 VJ collegium, Exhibit 3D484. Related to that, we say that General Pavkovic also violated the October Agreements because he directed his subordinate forces to engage in offensive actions against the KLA and misrepresented those in his reports, first of all, to the VJ General Staff by claiming that those were merely responses to initial attacks by the KLA. Let me turn now to the most significant contribution, joint VJ/MUP combat actions. During 1998, as the PRK commander and as a member of the Joint Command, Pavkovic commanded, planned, ordered, and coordinated joint VJ/MUP combat actions. In 1999, after he had been elevated to the 3rd Army command, he did the same and still in connection with the Joint Command, we say. In 1999 he continued to support MUP forces in those anti-terrorist actions, the same MUP forces which he well knew had committed crimes in 1998. This is set forth in much greater detail in our final brief at paragraphs 853 to 870. I want to talk about Pavkovic in the Joint Command, and I'll talk about several topics. First, this is the operations inter-departmental staff to suppress terrorism. We only have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise, interfering --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- and spoiling your eloquence. Now, from line 15 to line 19, you talked about General Pavkovic violating the October Agreement because he directed his subordinate forces to engage in offences against the KLA, misrepresenting those in his report, first of all, to the VJ General by claiming that those were merely responses to initial attacks by the KLA. Now, how do you formulate an accusation as to this because this is only focused on KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand your question correctly, part of the October Agreement provided that additional forces were not to be brought in and also that the OSCE was to be advised in advance when certain elements of the VJ were coming out of barracks or were going to engage in operations, and that's part of where we say he violated the agreements by bringing VJ elements out of barracks and engaging in offensive operations without prior notice to the verifiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Without prior notice. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're welcome. Now, let me return to Pavkovic and the Joint Command. The operations inter-departmental staff, we only have the one document P2166 that refers to that body, but I say we have other evidence showing the existence of that body and other meetings carried out by them. But before I go to that, I want to talk about other items joining Pavkovic with the Joint Command. We'll talk about the creation of the Joint Command. We'll talk about the 1998 plan to suppress terrorism. We'll talk about another one of my favourite exhibits P1468, the notes of Joint Command meetings; Exhibit P2166, the report on implementing the plan to suppress terrorism; and finally, evidence showing the continued existence of the Joint Command in 1999. Now, first the operations inter-departmental staff. Between late May 1998 and October 1998, we have evidence from the suspect interview of General Pavkovic that there were four what are basically described as top-level meetings of the VJ, MUP, and political brass about the crisis in Kosovo. The first meeting was about adopting the plan to suppress terrorism and forming a Joint Command. In General Pavkovic's interview at page 321, he indicates that the first meeting took place on the 30th of May, 1998, in Belgrade; the persons present were Milosevic, Milutinovic, Perisic, Jovica Stanisic from the state security, General Samardzic, General Dimitrijevic, and Pavkovic himself. And he then indicates that there was a second meeting, which we know was on the 21st of July, and at page 395 of his interview he tells us the third meeting took place on the 4th of August in 1998 in Belgrade. All the same persons were present except Jovica Stanisic. The fourth meeting took place on the 31st of October, and all the same persons were present. It's -- I'll address it when we come back to P2166, but you'll see Pavkovic tells us about four meetings of this group of high-ranking VJ, MUP, and political officials. You'll see in the October 29th meeting a numbering that would suggest that this is the fifth meeting of that group in October. Pavkovic tells us that the first meeting was about adopting the plan to suppress terrorism and forming a Joint Command. We'll look at that in just a minute in further detail. I'll talk about the creation, how did this body come into being, the creation of the Joint Command, according to Pavkovic, at pages 322 to 325 of his suspect interview, and if I could go to -- let me consult with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of our sources of information about the Joint Command was in the form of a response to an OTP request for assistance, and we received back from the Federal Ministry of Justice of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Exhibit P1317, which you see on your screen. They informed us in July 2002 that: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was formed on the order by the FRY President in June 1998 without any specific document ..." We have some evidence about the meeting of Mr. Milosevic's political party around June 10th, 1998, where some of our members of the Joint Command are named to go to Kosovo and deal with the situation. That seems to be the logical inference, that that is what this refers to, but as it indicates and as best as we have been able to determine, there is no document. And as we've said, there is no provision in the constitution that we could find or that Professor Markovic could help us with about provision for the existence of any such body. Note that this response says: "The above command operated until October of that year," 1998, "following which, several unofficial meetings were held where the current security situation was analysed ..." We don't have General Djakovica's notes or any equivalent regarding meetings after October 1998, but we do have a lot of evidence in this case suggesting that the Joint Command in some form continued to exist and function into 1999, and with General Vasiljevic's testimony we say that was still the case up until at least 1 June 1999. And it's not clear from this what distinguishes an official meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from an unofficial meeting, but that's what it says. It's interesting to note in this response, as well, that according to the military organ's knowledge, documents from the Joint Command related to military issues were delivered to the incumbent chief of the cabinet of the FRY president, and the buildings where those documents may have been housed were demolished and destroyed. But that raises more questions than it answers, I suggest, Your Honour, about, well, what other Joint Command documents were there that related to issues other than military issues and the fact that the documents may have been housed in destroyed buildings doesn't mean that they weren't housed elsewhere. But at any rate, that's the official response we had about the creation of the Joint Command from the Serbian government. But we have, perhaps, better evidence from General Pavkovic in his interview. Exhibit P949 from pages 322 to 326, he talks about how that came about. At page 322, he tells us about the first meeting. Among those present were himself and General Samardzic and General Perisic. The MUP representatives included General Djordjevic, Rade Markovic, Obrad Stevanovic, General Lukic. And on page 322 near the bottom, he tells us that the purpose of this first meeting was: "Adopting of the plan for fighting terrorism in Kosovo." And -- I'm sorry. It doesn't appear on your screen, but the B/C/S plan -- Pavkovic's B/C/S answer includes "i formiranje zajednicke komande." With my limited B/C/S, I understand that to mean forming Joint Command, which has not been translated into the English, but you'll see it in the original B/C/S. And then he goes on at page 324 to say that the result of the meeting was to start with realization of the plan for fighting terrorism. At 325, he tells us that the Joint Command was formed, at the bottom of the page. So it appears that this body, which I suggest to you was the inter -- the operations inter-departmental staff, created the Joint Command perhaps as early as that meeting in late May 1998. Other evidence related ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's concerning me, Mr. Hannis, is your reference to the foot of page 122 [sic] which you say can't be seen or isn't on the screen. Do we have that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 322?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it on my screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just not been picked up --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Here, it's mentioned as page 6 of 37 or something, but that is page 322 in e-court. You'll see the interpreter -- the biggest block for the interpreter about nine blocks up from the bottom, and immediately above that, Pavkovic's answer is the part where I'm referring to. Yes, that's it. You'll see the last four words: "I formiranje zajednicke komande."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any reason why that's not been interpreted at the time? I mean, the issue for me is whether this ought to be interpreted now. I understood that everything that was said in both languages was repeated in the other language, and you're founding on something which we can't read, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I could ask the interpreters to read those four words for us and interpret them for us, but I'm also satisfied because three pages later Pavkovic says the Joint Command was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that would be fine if that's what you're relying on, but what you're actually relying on is what's said earlier on this page, and therefore, that needs to be translated. So the best way of doing that is to ask the interpreter here now to read in English the last three words of that answer, which -- that interpreted answer, which is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm satisfied to have them read the whole statement of Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That might be better, so the passage immediately preceding what the interpreter says in B/C/S should now be read in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The purpose of that meeting was to adopt a plan for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and the setting up of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you content with that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any concern from you, Mr. Ackerman, about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the concern is the integrity of the rest of that document in view of that. It obviously has not been very carefully translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think there's a problem with the translation of the document. I think what happened was the interpreter, you'll see, asked Pavkovic a question about the earlier part of his answer, and I think so that's why he or she missed translating the rest of that into English at the time. I think if you review the entire document that there's not a grievous concern about the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, related to this, I would like you to take a look at an excerpt from the testimony of General Dimitrijevic when he was here testifying about what was happening in late May, June, and July regarding Kosovo. At -- and we talked about the Joint Command and Pavkovic. At this first meeting -- or this meeting in July had presented a plan that was apparently assigned to him to present at the first meeting. General Dimitrijevic says: "Why General Pavkovic? I was present, or rather, participated in a conversation at Milosevic's place when he called the Chief of General Staff," Perisic, "and me to discuss ..." He thought this was sometime in late May or perhaps mid- or late June, and Milosevic at that time had the idea that he presented to Perisic and Dimitrijevic about appointing Pavkovic the commander of all the forces in Kosovo, both the military and the MUP forces. Perisic and Dimitrijevic were opposed to that idea. He told you in his testimony that the simple reason they were opposed was because probably there would be obstruction and refusal on the part of the MUP to subordinate its units. I suggest to Your Honours, that's not a -- I'm not sure that was the real reason Perisic and Dimitrijevic were most concerned because if General Pavkovic is put in that position by Slobodan Milosevic, I suggest to you during that time and at that place, if that's what Milosevic wanted to do, he would make it happen, and he would make MUP go along with it if he wanted to force it that way, but he didn't. But keep all this in context. It's very important. I'll address this at the very end of my remarks. Keep all this evidence in context, review the evidence in chronological fashion, and you'll see all kinds of connections that may illuminate things which otherwise remain a bit confusing. At this same time, in June and July of 1998, we've seen some evidence that General Perisic was upset about how some VJ units were being used in Kosovo. We have the excerpt from one of those VJ collegiums. I don't have the precise cite in front of me, but July 1998 where he is upset because it's come to his attention that some VJ units had been used I think in the interior of Kosovo, despite his specific ban on use of VJ units without his specific permission. And you heard the evidence from General Dimitrijevic that General Samardzic had tried to implement disciplinary proceedings against General Pavkovic in connection with that, and what happens instead, there's no discipline, and Pavkovic is promoted by Mr. Milosevic. We have evidence of that promotion in Exhibit P1510, which is a newspaper report from Tanjug, saying that Milosevic had promoted Pavkovic from major-general to lieutenant-general. That's the very same day that they had the meeting of what I say was the inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism, where the plan for suppressing terrorism was first discussed. I suggest to you that this is the way that Milosevic got what he wanted in effect by creating this Joint Command with one of his personal representatives, Mr. Sainovic, to play a leading role, and he then didn't have to go directly in the face of General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic. Although we say he could, I think the evidence suggests that until that time that was something he didn't want to do. Remember, then, two days later, on the 23rd of July, 1998, is when General Perisic writes his letter to General Milosevic complaining about how the army is being used and in his view being misused contrary to the constitution in his view, how persons outside the military are having a role in directing how army units are used, et cetera. And Pavkovic's status now in connection with this Joint Command, do you remember what General Dimitrijevic said about that? He thought part of the reason that this Joint Command was created was so that Pavkovic could point to something that he had behind him, and what he had behind him in the Joint Command was Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milosevic. So that's how we say Mr. Milosevic arranged to get what he wanted in the first place, which in effect was to have Pavkovic in charge of all the forces in Kosovo. Reflective on this, the plan to suppress terrorism, we'll take a quick look at Exhibits 4D100 and 4D101 and then 1468 and 2166. 4D100 and 4D101 on the 22nd and 23rd of July. One day after this meeting with Milosevic where the plan to suppress terrorism was discussed, Pavkovic in 4D100 sends to his superior, General Samardzic, the 3rd Army commander, a request for clarification about engagement of the Pristina Corps units. You'll see he makes reference in that document to the meeting with President Milosevic, and he reflects that an order was given to implement the plan for combatting terrorist forces. The plan envisages the participation of the MUP and Pristina Corps units, and his last line said: "In view of the above, please work out in more detail the engagement of the Pristina Corps units in implementation of the plan." I think I made the comment the first time we brought this document up in evidence that at least to my layman's eye that reads more like a document from a superior to a subordinate than vice versa, but that's just my opinion. 4D101, that is from Samardzic -- or from Pavkovic to Samardzic the next day, the 23rd of July. He notes that implementation of the second stage of the plan to eliminate terrorism provides for the engagement of MUP and PRK units. He reminds Samardzic: "You have been briefed on the plan as a whole several times, the last time at the briefing with the president on 21 July when the order was given to commence implementation of the plan." Now, Pavkovic is very much, we say, encouraged by the creation of this Joint Command and this plan to suppress terrorism and his role in all of that. Look at -- look carefully, I request of you, in your review of the evidence before writing your judgement at P1468, General Djakovica's notes of the Joint Command meeting. Because of the handwriting, there are several parts that unfortunately we weren't able to have translated. They're illegible, and apparently even now some of them are illegible to the one who wrote them, but there is enough there that you can get the sense and the gist of what happened in those 60-plus meetings between July and October 1998. We say they clearly show this group is more than just an information-sharing body as some of the witnesses would have you believe. The members themselves refer to it as a "command," and what is discussed at the meeting is corroborated by events on the ground and by contemporaneous documents from the MUP and VJ. If you could have a look at an excerpt from these meeting notes, first of all, page 160 of P1468, Mr. Sainovic, this is on the 26th of October which you will recall is the day after the Clark-Naumann agreement was reached and signed, where Mr. Milosevic made his comment about a final solution in the spring. Sainovic is advising the Joint Command members about what's been happening, and you'll see he says: "When pulling out we must be careful enough not to let anyone find out that parts of some detachments did not pull out." That relates to our earlier points about violating the October Agreements and the approach to dealing with the OSCE. But right below that, you see General Pavkovic says: "My command from Nis," the 3rd Army command, "believes that this command," the Joint Command, not the joint coordinating committee or not the joint information-sharing body, the Joint Command, "this command should cease to exist." But on the next page and the next excerpt -- and I'm sorry, I don't think I have the right one on the screen. The very next page, I'll read from it in case I can't find it to put up for you. It's at page 61 and -- 161 in the English version in e-court. Again, from this 26th of October meeting Mr. Sainovic says: "This stage of combat operation is to be closed, and decisions and tasks are to be given. I think that with OSCE pressure there should be more coordination between all the bodies." This is where you'll recall Andjelkovic then says: "Nobody's authorised to take away our documents. All the documents are to be kept on the Joint Command's premises." Then Mr. Sainovic, then, finally the last comment noted from this meeting says: "Since the command was not able to keep the documents in the district building, conditions have been created to keep the documents in a MUP building." And then finally, the one last reference is from a meeting on the 28th of October, and I think we do have this one. Yeah, it's General Pavkovic, page 163. One thing I wanted this up for was General Pavkovic's reference to: "We have to take into consideration how to use the armed population and how to involve it in the defence of communications." We'll relate to this later when we're talking about the armed non-Siptar population. But on this topic I'm talking about right now, Minister Minic is talking about this command. You'll see his last four lines: "I think that this command should stay and work with the same people until the end of the year and meet in accordance to the need. The documentation should be completed and given to the military committee of the President of the FRY." This is from the 28th of October, and we say, Your Honour, that this relates to the big meeting that was held the next day on the 29th of October of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism which is reflected in Exhibit P2166. But you'll see Sainovic, Pavkovic, Minic, Andjelkovic, all referring to themselves as a command, as the Joint Command, not the coordinating body but the Joint Command. P2166, the report on the work of the Joint Command. We say this document demonstrates the existence and the nature of the Joint Command, particularly in regard to the 1998 and the summer plan to suppress terrorism. You see in that report itself that the participants agree, and the conclusion pronounced by Mr. Milosevic at the end is that the Joint Command should continue to function. It was Mr. Sainovic himself who suggested that perhaps in a different state, maybe with fewer persons involved, but that it should continue. In that document, you'll also see the explanation for why no state of emergency was declared and an awareness about civilian casualties in the event of mobilisation and engaging strong forces. Let's take a look at the next slide. I just put this up for you to see the number on this document, DT. I think it's state secret. This is number 208-5, and that's my argument, Your Honour, that dash 5 means that this is the fifth one; this is the fifth meeting. The first was May 30th, the second was July 21st, one on August 4th or 5th, one on August 31st, and then this one on the 5th of -- or this one on the 29th of October. And this is part of the reason that I suggest to you those four meetings described by General Pavkovic in his suspect interview were meetings of the operations inter-departmental staff. And in 2166 you see the list of all the persons who were attending that meeting. The next slide, please. This is General Pavkovic explaining about the implementation of the plan to suppress terrorism and explaining some of the restrictions they had to take into consideration. One was avoiding provoking an excessive reaction from abroad and carrying out the above without proclaiming a state of emergency. He then explains why an introduction of a state of emergency was not acceptable for several reasons. Keep in mind General Perisic's letter of 23 July 1998, P717, where he had urged the president to impose or declare one of those states or to have that done by the appropriate body so that the army then could be engaged more fully. Pavkovic explains, Well, first we would provoke a reaction from the foreign countries which would intervene militarily on behalf of the terrorists. Second, we'd have to mobilise the VJ and that could cause a problem domestically; we're not even sure mobilisation would be successful. Third, the engagement of strong forces would draw more attention from domestic and international public, and certainly it would have. We've already had two UN resolutions prior to this date decreeing the use of force against the civilian population and since the terrorists would sustain extensive losses as would our own forces, and avoiding civilian casualties would not be possible. So Pavkovic and everyone at this meeting, then, we say, Your Honour, is on notice that engaging in that activity was going to unavoidably result in civilian casualties, but that's what they did anyway. They went ahead in 1999 and did that. It's interesting to note the next comment. I'm not sure why this was put in there at this meeting, but Pavkovic says: "As may be concluded, our plan was not to 'kill all the Siptars' or expel them from KiM, but to destroy the main terrorist forces and separate the terrorists from the people." We suggest that perhaps in light of what had happened in 1995 there was an awareness of the problem of taking that approach of killing all the Siptars, and to try and expel all the Siptars from Kosovo at that point in time we say would have been extremely difficult in light of the intense international awareness and focus of what was happening in Kosovo. And we'll argue this again, probably more than once before we're done. We are not alleging in our indictment or claiming that the plan was to expel all the Albanians from Kosovo; it was only to expel a sufficient number in order to maintain Serbian control of the province, as a practical matter during the war, and you'll see this in General Pavkovic's interview himself. There was an awareness that once NATO started bombing there was some strategic considerations regarding keeping part of the civilian population in Kosovo. If all the civilians were kicked out of Kosovo, the only people remaining would have been the VJ and the MUP, and NATO bombing would have been much more intense and wide open, we suggest. So in October, the end of October 1998, in discussing the plan that had been implemented prior to that day, Pavkovic notes that it wasn't our plan then, at the time, to kill all the Siptars or expel them. But, Your Honour, this is part of my argument that I've made, that there -- because of the Kosovo problem there were ever more oppressive measures to try and deal with the situation. They continually met with failure. They still had the problem. So after October 29th, 1998, we say they had to do try something more severe than they had done up to now, and that was to increase their military and police actions and remove as many Kosovo Albanians as they could, including the civilians. Because you see, the problem was to separate the terrorists from the people. You've heard lots of evidence about the difficulty with that, how the terrorists would throw down their weapons and change into civilian clothes and go into the villages. It was a practical impossibility, and we say they decided, the heck with that. We can't sort this out anymore. We're going to deport -- or we're going to kick out as many of these people as we can, because half of them support these guys anyhow. They provide them food, shelter, et cetera. Next slide, please. Next, in P2166 there's a note about what tasks were set forth in the plan, and one was arming the Serbian and Montenegrin people and establishing reserve police units to defend villages. This relates to P1415 that we showed you earlier and discussions in the VJ collegiums. Next. Disarming all the Siptar Albanian villages. Next. The moving out of non-Albanians was prevented. This was, again, we say part of the plan to try to maintain Serb control of the province to keep the Serbs in Kosovo and remove as big a number of the Albanians as possible to achieve that ultimate goal of maintaining control. Next. We say this project -- this plan to suppress terrorism had been a last-ditch effort to try and solve the Kosovo problem before the October Agreements took place and the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived to Kosovo. I've discussed Pavkovic's comment about the plan was not to kill all, but we say the new year 1999 called for a new plan because this one in the light of what happened after October 1998 proved not to be successful. The KLA came back just as strong or stronger than ever. Next. Now, we have a number of statements that we say imply that there, indeed, was a plan. We've talked earlier about Milosevic's comments on the 24th of October, 1998, talking about a final solution. You heard, I think, when Mr. Stamp was talking about Mr. Milutinovic's statement, and in our brief we have a reference to Mr. Stambuk's statements about massacres in Kosovo if NATO bombs. Next. We have Mr. Seselj on the eve of the war. We played this one for you: "If NATO bombs us, we Serbs will suffer casualties, but no Albanians will be left in Kosovo." I think we played this when Professor Markovic was here, and you'll recall Professor Seselj was a member of the government, one of the deputy prime ministers at the time, and that was what he said on the eve of the war. Next, please. Now, we've had a number of witnesses come in and claim that there was no plan, a whole parade of military, police, and civilian witnesses from -- called by the Defence who claimed that there was no plan. I'll say there's something that they all have in common. One of -- one or more of these three factors are listed on the slide. They have a personal motive to lie about that, to protect themselves or their colleagues and friends or the institutions of which they were a member, whether it be the VJ or the MUP or the Serbian Yugoslav government at the time; or 2, they were not told about the plan or were not in a position to know about it. And as I think you heard, one of our state security witnesses, I think it was Mr. Mijatovic called by the Pavkovic -- or by the Sainovic Defence talked about -- in security work there's this principle of need to know, and you only tell people what they need to know. And many of the people in the VJ and MUP who were involved in implementing the actions that resulted in the crimes on the ground would not necessarily have to be told about the plan in order for them to do their job. In thirdly, some of those people who denied that there were a plan were merely speculating based on inadequate information. They were at such a low level or in such a job or only there at an earlier time where they were not in a position to really know whether or not there was a plan. Next. Now, let me talk about the continuation of the Joint Command because there's been -- first there was an argument there wasn't a Joint Command; well, okay, there was, but it was only a coordinating body, and it only worked up until October 1998. But we say the evidence shows, no, no; it continued on through the 1st of June, 1999, at least. You saw in Exhibit P2166, the minutes of the inter-departmental staff meeting, that the conclusion was the participants agreed that the Joint Command should continue to function. P1197 is one of those Joint Command operations report, and I think that's from November of 1998, so it shows the Joint Command continued to exist. P2945 was the interview of Colonel Stojanovic, the newspaper article which included a report he had written to the Joint Command about the security situation. The VJ collegium of 21 January 1999 where there's discussion about the events at Racak. You'll see that there was a reference -- a couple of references to the Joint Command by General Ojdanic in talking about what had happened down there. Then we have a number of Joint Command orders in March and April 1999. General Lazarevic testified and told us about those and his explanation of, Well, no, no, those were really Pristina Corps orders even though they do say Joint Command on the top and they do say at the bottom that the Joint Command will command these actions. In addition, there are references to Joint Command in VJ documents at all levels, at the Supreme Command Staff level, at the 3rd Army level, and at the Pristina Corps level. P1487, P2017, and P2016 are some examples of that. 2016 is a 25 April 1999 combat report from the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, to both the 3rd Army command and the Supreme Command Staff. On page 2 of that document under activities of the Pristina Corps unit, it notes: "Operations of combing the terrain and breaking up Siptar terrorist forces continue in line with the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." The 29th of April, we see Exhibit P2017, which is from General Pavkovic in the 3rd Army command to the Supreme Command Staff reporting on events the day before, and at page 2 it mentions that measures were undertaken to block the above sectors and carry out tasks in line with the Joint Command decision or the Joint Command for Kosovo decision. In addition, as I indicated before, we have the testimony of General Vasiljevic about the 1st of June meeting. With regard to General Pavkovic himself, in his suspect interview he makes reference to the fact that there were at least a couple of informal meetings of the Joint Command in 1999, and General Lukic in his suspect interview made reference to meetings of the Joint Command in 1999, including after the start of the NATO campaign. Finally, P1317 which we looked at earlier, the RFA response from Yugoslavia noted several unofficial meetings after October 1998. All of this evidence we say clearly shows that the Joint Command continued to exist up to and including the 1st of March. Next. Pavkovic arranged a number of arguments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that a deliberate reference to the 1st of March, or was that a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was supposed to be the 1st of June. If I said March, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the Defence arguments are that there's no 7(1) liability because he had no criminal intent. He didn't plan, order, instigate, or aid and abet any crimes. He didn't know of any. We say that the totality of the evidence and as detailed in our closing brief makes it clear that that's not the case. He denies participation in the JCE except by one of the excluded means. We think that's not a correct understanding of the law. He claims no link to the direct perpetrators, but we say the law doesn't necessarily require that, but we also say that he did have a direct link to the perpetrators because those forces were in his chain of command. The Defence -- the military accused have tried to I think conjure up a bit of a straw man in saying, Well, my guy was nine levels removed from the squad member who carried out that crime. Well, yeah, but that's a little bit exaggerated. I think that should be condensed a little, and we're talking about two or three levels primarily. But you've seen from the VJ collegiums and from the combat reports and from the orders going up and down the chain that the high levels, they were well-informed about what was going on. You've seen at some of these VJ collegium, they're discussing fairly minute events and incidents. It's strange credibility to believe that they didn't know about these, and clearly Pavkovic knew about crimes being committed. You see in our brief and you've heard the evidence about when he was summoned to speak to General Ojdanic, Vasiljevic, and Gajic at that middle-of-May meeting to discuss crimes that apparently had been stuck in the bottle-neck of the 3rd Army and not reported up the Supreme Command Staff prior to that date. And Pavkovic comes to that meeting and talks about how he's had conversations with General Lukic and there are 800 bodies above the ground in Kosovo not accounted for and the army takes responsibility -- or at least the army concedes that 200-and-some of those bodies were in their area of operations and 300-and-some were in MUP's and the others, and nobody was claiming any responsibility for. So he knew about it. He knew about crimes. And no plan, and we've talked about that, and no 7(3), no effective control over the MUP. We say if you accept that he didn't have any effective control over the MUP, in one way he at least failed to prevent future crimes by continuing to order his VJ units to support the MUP, support MUP units which he had knowledge had committed crimes in the past. And by his own document, P1459, the 25 May 1999 report about which there's much controversy about whether that was indeed written at that time and sent up the chain at that time, but in which he indicates that MUP units and MUP members were committing crimes against Albanian civilians: Murder, rape, looting, robbery. And yet, after May 23rd, the VJ continued on several occasions to support MUP units engaged in anti-terrorist operations, combat actions. I think it's in evidence Colonel Kotur's order regarding Operation Sekac directing MUP units to engage in those actions. Inadequate measures were taken as regard Pavkovic's VJ subordinate units when he was aware of crimes, and that's detailed in our written brief. Regarding the next slide -- well, I'm sorry, before we get to General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before you move on can I ask you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- one thing there that I've been trying to figure out. Page 26, line 17, when you're summarizing General Pavkovic's position: "He denies participation in the JCE except by the excluded means. We think that is not a correct understanding of the law." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think in General Pavkovic's brief he argued that -- may I grab my binder? There was a bit of a confusing argument to me, and perhaps Mr. Ackerman can help me with the paragraph -- all right. I'm sorry. Your Honour, at paragraph 42, page 12, of Pavkovic's final brief, he said: "The allegation that Pavkovic committed acts by his participation in joint criminal enterprise requires the Prosecution to prove that he was a perpetrator of the acts." He says: "One who 'commits' is a direct perpetrator of the act. Any other interpretation would change the JCE concept from a theory of liability into a new criminal offence. That he planned, instigated, ordered, or aided and abetted is specifically excluded by the indictment from JCE consideration." And he goes on and says: "It's very difficult to imagine what it is the Prosecution contends that Pavkovic could have done from his position as 3rd Army commander that would constitute a JCE commission of a crime excluding planning, instigating, ordering, or aiding and abetting in the process." So I read that to mean that he was suggesting that the only way that Pavkovic could have committed anything was by planning, instigating, ordering, or aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he may be saying, firstly, that your indictment only alleges that his role in the JCE was in relation to commission, and he may also be saying that the law confines the conduct that a person may be responsible for as part of a JCE to something that can be described as commission. In paragraph 18 of your indictment you say: "By using the word 'committed' the Prosecutor does not intend to suggest that any of the accused physically perpetrated any of the crimes. Committing in this indictment when used in relation to the accused refers to participation in a joint criminal enterprise as a co-perpetrator, either directly or indirectly."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't understand the law to say that commission cannot include planning, instigating, ordering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your argument is that you can as a planner commit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: An act that is a contribution to the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's something that the jurisprudence doesn't really make clear at the moment; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So by reference -- I was really concerned about the reference to the excluded means, and that's what I thought it was, but I wanted to be clear about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just give me one moment before you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A few more points raised in Pavkovic's written submission that I wanted to address before moving on to General Lazarevic. One claim is the fact that some people were allowed to stay shows that there was no plan. As I said before, we're not alleging that the intention of the accused was to expel the entire population, only a substantial portion. And we say 700 to 800.000 is a substantial portion of that population. Another argument asserted is that the perpetrators were not VJ, so my guy, Pavkovic, is innocent. First of all, we're saying that the VJ and the MUP acted in coordination. This is a JCE case. We have argued that the direct perpetrators were either members of the JCE and shared the intent or they were used by the members of the JCE. We say it's sufficient for you as the Trial Chamber to find that a link existed between the direct perpetrators and one member of the JCE, either VJ or MUP. And in the alternative to our JCE charge, we've charged the military accused with aiding and abetting. They lent material and moral support to the perpetrators of the crimes who were not the VJ. By implementing instructions received from Ojdanic and through his involvement in the Joint Command, Pavkovic lent material and moral support to the perpetrators of the crimes. Now, with that I would now turn to General Lazarevic. General Lazarevic, I see he's not here today, he was the Pristina Corps commander, Chief of Staff in 1998. During that time he attended at least five Joint Command meetings as we see from P1468. He signed the decision for the Slup-Voksa Joint Command -- joint action with the MUP in August 1998 that was to be commanded by the Joint Command, and he was the Pristina Corps commander then, in 1999 [sic], and he told you he or his staff drafted those Joint Command orders that we see in March and April 1999 from which we say the crimes alleged in the indictment flowed. He contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by commanding, planning, ordering, and coordinating activities of the Pristina Corps and subordinate units in Kosovo. He implemented the Joint Command orders. He coordinated joint VJ and MUP combat actions in both 1998 and 1999. He participated in incorporating volunteers into the Pristina Corps. With regard to his command of the Pristina Corps, first of all we note that the Pristina Corps chain of command functioned well, with orders going down the chain to subordinate units and reports coming back up. Later on, Lazarevic exercised control over the subordinated military territorial detachments, and some of those units engaged in combat. This is set forth in more detail in our written brief at paragraphs 926 to 932, and one example of the military district or the military territorial detachments being engaged in combat is found in Exhibit 5D1074 from the 15th of April, 1999. You'll see a reference to that. Next slide. We say he implemented Joint Command orders. First of all, he attended some of those Joint Command meetings in 1998. He signed the decision for the Voksa action in August 1998 that was to be commanded by the Joint Command, and then he told you that he and his staff drafted those Joint Command orders which are reflected in the maps we showed you earlier in describing the pattern of the crimes committed in March and April of 1999. Next slide. He coordinated joint VJ and MUP combat. He told us that there was full cooperation and coordination of the VJ and the MUP in both 1998 and 1999. One of the prime examples of this in 1999 was described yesterday when I was talking to you about General Ojdanic and his directive regarding Grom 3. We saw that come from Ojdanic and the supreme -- I'm sorry, the General Staff at that time down to Pavkovic, who then issued his own Grom 3 order, and Lazarevic in P2808 on the 16th of February issued his own version of that to subordinate brigades. And those directions, those orders, were seen and carried out at the ground level. You heard testimony from Colonel Zivaljevic from the MUP, how he saw the contents of those orders in his meetings with Colonel Gergar and when he saw the map excerpt, and those actions were carried out. Djakovic also told you how Exhibit 6D716 from the 17th of February, 1999, was drafted by him to help MUP in knowing how to write these kind of orders up. And in Exhibit P1990, the MUP staff meeting for the 17th of February, 1999, you will recall, I think it's at page 2, there's a reference to: "Staff plans once ordered to carry out three mopping-up operations in Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas." And it noted that they had allotted 4.000 police, 70 OPG and 900 reservists for that eventuality, which we say then did occur later on, and that was part of what happened in early -- or in late March 1999 after the onset of the NATO air-strikes and resulted in the crimes charged in our indictment. P1503 is a Pristina Corps order of 27 May 1999 to crush and destroy the Siptar terrorists in the Prekaze sector. I put this one out because this relates to the argument I was raising earlier. It's addressed to the command of the MUP. It was signed by Lazarevic only three days after he wrote his own report in Exhibit P1723 on the 24th of May to Pavkovic, complaining about the conduct of the MUP, particularly at the mixed check-points, and how the MUP were engaging in crimes against civilians. And in spite of that, three days later, in spite of this problem, he's calling for joint action with the MUP. Next slide. We say that Lazarevic was also a contributor to the joint criminal enterprise by incorporating volunteers into the VJ. He directly was involved in approving and assigning volunteers. He had notice of their greater propensity for criminal behaviour, and yet still as of 18 April 1999 the Pristina Corps had at least 1.259 volunteers under Lazarevic's command. Exhibit 5D825 is a combat report of the 175th Brigade, infantry brigade. It's dated the 31st of March, 1999, and if we could go to the next slide, I think we actually have an excerpt from that document. This is from Colonel Petrovic to the Pristina Corps command, and he notes: "After certain volunteers showed indiscipline and other criminal activities, the situation is slowly becoming more stable. Eight volunteers for whom there are reasonable grounds to suspect that they committed the crime in Zegra village have been arrested." We heard some details about that crime and a number of murders and robberies that were committed by volunteers in the 175th. I note that Colonel Petrovic tells us that: "The commander of the Pristina Corps," General Lazarevic, "approved the sending of 24 volunteers who wanted to be immediately involved in combat operations to the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. Some said they wanted to go back home and they'll be disarmed and taken back. There are 32 of them so far. Some volunteers said they wanted to link up with their sons ... and their requests shall be met." I say this may relate to something you saw in one of the evening briefings where General Gajic was reporting about a situation with volunteers with which there had been some problems and had been sent back. But this shows that General Lazarevic was aware of volunteers and approved where they would be sent, in this case to the 243rd so they could immediately be involved in combat operations. There's another portion of this I want to refer you to, same document. Colonel Petrovic notes that: "Since there are in the zone of responsibility of the brigade very many units and armed individuals which have not been included in the initial decision received from the Pristina Corps command, we ask that you give us information about all units whose deployment in the zone of the 175th Infantry Brigade have been approved by you so that we can engage our forces properly ..." So this is notice to General Lazarevic about the forces that are within the areas of responsibility of his subordinate units. This relates to the arguments from the Defence about perpetrators and the suggestion that there are rogue elements perhaps engaged in these crimes. As Ms. Kravetz said from the pattern of the crimes and as we showed you on the map reflecting Colonel Delic's post-action analysis in the area of Bela Crkva, Celina, Mala Krusa, et cetera, there were no other significant bodies of armed men speaking Serbian and committing these crimes other than VJ and MUP and individuals under the control of our accused. 4D371 is a Pristina Corps combat report from the 1st of April, 1999. It notes the security situation is stable, but "impaired to some degree by incidents of crime ..." And also: "Volunteers, reserve contingents of the military territorial detachments and free individuals have the greatest influence on incidents of crime." Notice, too, evidence indicating that General Lazarevic was aware of the presence of these individuals and the propensity for criminal activity by such persons. 5D215 is another Pristina Corps combat report from the 18th of April, 1999, which reflects that there were 1.259 volunteers in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps command on that day. General Lazarevic raises some of the same kinds of defence arguments that Pavkovic and Ojdanic did, first of all, saying there were no crimes by VJ units, that there was no plan, no participation in the JCE, and no 7(3) responsibility. We address all of those in much greater detail in our written submission. But next, I have to make a comment about General Lazarevic. You have to deal with the issue of his credibility. We say he was not completely candid with you about everything. In particular, I suggest to you that he was not completely candid about the Joint Command, about his knowledge of the Joint Command and his role or his participation with the Joint Command. You saw what he said in his initial interview with Mr. Coo when he first came to The Hague, and perhaps it was only a matter of memory, but he had to be shown documents with his name on them before he came to remember that he had gone to, perhaps, a Joint Command meeting or two or three or, as it turned out, actually five in 1998. And for me, one of the most compelling incidents of what I suggest was not complete candor with you related to Exhibits P1966 and P1967. These are the Joint Command orders number 455-56 and 455-56/1. I think they're both dated the 22nd of March, 1999, just a couple of days before the war began, calling for operations to crush the Siptar terrorists I think in the Malo Kosovo area. And 1966 is a Joint Command order; no signature at the end, just the typewritten "Joint Command." 1967 is signed by Lazarevic, and that's the one that's entitled Amendment To 455-56 or Exhibit P1966. 1966 has the full complement that you see in these standard orders from item 1 through 12, you know, describing the enemy and the neighbours and the task and logistical support and command and control, et cetera. The amendment only has I think items 4 and 5, what's been decided in the task for the assigned units. We discussed that with General Lazarevic, and he explained, Well, when you're doing an amendment you don't re-write the whole thing; you only change the part that needed to be changed. And he explained what needed to be changed was I think the date or the time for commencing the operation, and there was some change in the specific task as to where a unit started from and perhaps which unit was going to do a part of the action. And so I said, Well, then, you sign this amendment titled "Joint Command," you made no change to the original, 1966, which called for these actions to be commanded by the Joint Command; and the argument I tried to put to him was, So therefore you see no need to make a change in the order and you agree that these operations should be commanded by the Joint Command? And he explained to me, he said, No, no, no, that wasn't necessary because, you see, I had changed the command post, and anybody would know that the Pristina Corps command was at that command post. But if you look at that document, that's not correct. P1966 indicated where the command post from which the actions were to be commanded would be, and I think it said the peacetime location of the Pristina Corps command. But in the amendment for each unit that is engaged, there's a separate command post, which is typical in these orders. If there's the 125th Brigade, there's going to be a command post from where they run their operations. He tried to argue that the command post for the Pristina Corps was in the same place as the command post for the 354th Brigade. And when he said that I thought, Oh, gosh, maybe he's right. But then I looked at it and, no, that's not true, and there's no way someone receiving that order would know that the Pristina Corps command was commanding that whole operation from the command post for the 354th when Colonel Zivanovic came here to testify, commander of the 125th, we showed him those two documents and asked him that, and he told you that, no, from this he wouldn't know where the command post was. Also, I think General Lazarevic was not honest with you about the armed non-Siptar population and the inclusion in many of those directives and orders to engage the armed non-Siptar population in carrying out those tasks, in defending the non-Siptar settlements and population and otherwise. He tried to explain to say that term was really sort of an artefact left over from earlier days when they used to have All People's Defence as part of this system, and that, really, it was only the civil defence and/or the civil protection. I think he sort of waffled on his answer on that. I asked him to explain, Well, why didn't you just say that? His answer was, Well, I get my order from above, and I can't change that part of the order. Yesterday when we talked about the April 9th directive from General Ojdanic down to Pavkovic and Grom 4, you saw that General Lazarevic had written his version of Grom 4 four days before he got any written order from Pavkovic about that, and in General Lazarevic's version he writes, "Engage the armed non-Siptar population. So I suggest to you, he knew better who that was, but he didn't want to tell you about that. Another area that I'm not sure how that falls out relates to Meja. You've had the testimony of Nike Peraj about General Lazarevic being present in the area where those operations took place at the end of April 1999, and there was detailed information by the Defence to rebut Nike Peraj and say, He must be lying about that, that can't be true because I, General Lazarevic, was not there on that day. The day before, I was in Pristina at this awards ceremony, et cetera, et cetera. There are a couple of possibilities here; one is that Nike Peraj could be off by a day, but we also have evidence that General Lazarevic was in that area on I think the 28th of April. In the combat report of the 125th Motorised Brigade, it notes that General Lazarevic is at their location. Zivanovic told us where that was, and it's in the area. They say that Lazarevic was there between I think 9.00 in the morning and 12.00 noon, but the Defence presented another exhibit that shows General Lazarevic some many kilometres away, I suggest perhaps an hour away, at 9.00 because he notes some commander from some element of the 37th Brigade stuck in a motor vehicle in the creek, and he sends a warning to all others not to be -- about that. So either he can be at two places in one time or there's something not right with those documents. And P1723, the report from Lazarevic to Pavkovic about the MUP crimes, this I'm afraid, Your Honour, is still a bit of mystery for me. I don't know how Your Honours are going to deal with P1723 on the 24th of May and P1459 on the 25th of May, which is Pavkovic's report about the MUP committing crimes and that evidence suggesting that the document was put into archives after the fact, and there are a couple possibilities. In the end, I don't know that it makes any difference on your final judgement in this case, but it is an issue that we all have to contend with, and it's there. Perhaps Lazarevic wrote his report on that date and sent it up and Pavkovic didn't write his until later. Perhaps Lazarevic and Pavkovic worked together in doing that. Perhaps both documents were back-dated. There is an issue, not only with Pavkovic's P1459 and what we see from the archives of the Supreme Command Staff, but with regard to Lazarevic's exhibit, P1723, there is something with the numbering of that document. It has a routing number, and we saw in the 455 series of documents that there are two 455 numbers with -- documents with the same number, and oddly enough, one of those is that 24 May report. He certainly would have a motive not to tell you the truth about that if he was involved in the joint criminal enterprise. He's not going to take the stand and tell you that's the case. He's not going to sit through two years of trial when he could tell you that at the beginning and be judged guilty and move on from that. He can't have enjoyed our company that much. Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Next, I wanted to speak briefly connected to the armed non-Siptar population. We have Joint Command instructions for the defence of populated inhabited areas. These documents came out in late July 1998, and they're referred to as the Joint Command instructions. Your Honours, I have about four different documents I want to show you. Perhaps we could take the break a couple minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We shall do that, Mr. Hannis, and we'll resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to go quickly through this next section. I was going to cover it in more detail, but I think in the interest of time for Mr. Stamp and for my final remarks, I'll speed up. I did want to talk about Joint Command instructions for the defence of populated and inhabited areas. We did discuss this with some witness who came in. P2086, 1064, 1063, 1065, and 1067 are a series of documents from late July 1998 relating to this, and it sheds some light, we say, on the issue of the armed non-Siptar population, the reserve police, the civil protection, the civil defence, exactly who these people were and how they fit into the system. I'm not going to take the time now to go into the specific details of each of those documents, and as I say they are from late July 1998, but we see we had no evidence indicating that these instructions changed or were not still in effect at the time that the crimes occurred in March, April, and later in 1999. And I think they're consistent with the evidence from some of the crime base witnesses who talked about seeing some of their local labourers in uniforms and at the scene when some of the crimes occurred. So I would urge Your Honours to look at those exhibits in some further detail when you are reaching your judgement in this case. So I'll ask Mr. Reid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred to these as Joint Command instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit P2086 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we just see that one as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. We can show you that one. It's in Sanction, I think, P2086. It is entitled: "The instructions for the defence of inhabited places," and you'll see at the top it says: "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." I don't know if you have it on your screen yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, it looks like you have the B/C/S version on the left. And 2086, we say, is the item that is referred to in the cover letter, P1064, and it refers to the instructions as having been issued by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. If you want to see P1064 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. That's all that's required, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll ask Mr. Reid if we can fast-forward to the exhibit regarding Izbica. I did want to go into just a little detail about Izbica and about Meja and Korenica. Izbica, you've heard testimony from Mr. Thaqi and Mustafa Draga and a few other witnesses about the crimes that occurred at Izbica, and in connection with that, I would ask you to look at Exhibit P1968, was a Joint Command order for operations in that area. That Joint Command order is dated the 24th of March, 1999, and it bears confidential number 455-73. And if you look at the task for the various units to be engaged in that operation, we have drawn on the map where those units were located and where their movements were to take place. The first slide we will show you is where Izbica is located, and this is in the Drenica sector. The next item we'd like to show you, those circles -- these are the five different VJ units or elements of VJ units that were involved in this Joint Command order, and the circles show the locations from which they were starting. The next slide, we show you where their movement was to take place according to the Joint Command order. And you'll see that these operations are pushing -- it seems to me, it's logical that it would be pushing the -- civilian population in a direction to move away from these, and that's consistent with the testimony of the crime base witnesses, and you'll see the elements of the 37th Brigade moving right by Izbica. You can look at the map in Exhibit P615 for scale, and those last two yellow circles regarding Tactical Group 252, I think the bottom one is for the village of Vosnjak, or maybe it's the top one. I can't read that on my map here, but that's less -- that's a kilometre, basically, or less from Izbica. And you saw in one of the daily combat reports from the 37th Motorised Brigade that the day before the crimes happened in Izbica that they requested instructions from the Pristina Corps command about what to do because they anticipated to come across thousands of civilian refugees. But the following day there's no report; there's no mention of that. So we ask you to take a look at that evidence, have a look on this map, and we say this clearly shows that the only forces in that area at that time were the VJ and MUP forces carrying out actions in coordination with the instructions from the Joint Command in P1968. The circles are locations specified in the Joint Command order as areas where the Siptar terrorist forces are to be destroyed. And the lines and the arrow show the direction and axis of movement for those specific units. And with regard to Meja and Korenica, I just ask you to recall the testimony of some of the victim witnesses from that area. On the screen you have a picture of Lizane Malaj who testified for you early in this case. She testified about her husband and son being taken out of the house and shot in their front yard while she was then told to go to Albania, go down the road, and she told you about her journey leaving Kosovo subsequent to the killings of her family members. Next slide, please. This is a map that we saw with Nike Peraj, but it was also I think corroborated by witness K-73, and we heard about that operation, which was a joint VJ and MUP operation. It included elements of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, moving from the north/north-west, in a south/south-easterly direction, and we heard from the insider witness about how they were directed to expel people from their homes, and that's consistent with what Lizane Malaj, Merita Dedaj, Martin Pnishi and other witnesses have told you about that operation at the end of April, 1999. The next map. This is a map showing Korenica, and the markings made on here in blue and red were made by Colonel Vukovic - or then, at the time of the event, Major Vukovic - of the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 549th. And we saw some documents concerning where his unit was located and what their tasks were on that day and put him at the graveyard at the outskirts of Korenica. As you know from the evidence and looking at the map, Korenica is not a big place, and I suggest to you there is no way that he could have been at that location on that date as he's marked on the map and not been aware of what was happening at Korenica to Lizane Malaj and her family and the others and the shootings that were going on in the village and the killings that were occurring and the women and children being directed down the road. He denied seeing anything like that, but I suggest to you that that is impossible and that he had a motive not to be truthful to you about that and that you should be highly suspect of his testimony. We had some evidence that he himself had been subject of a military judicial proceeding in connection with his directing one of his subordinates to make a false entry about the use of 30 litres of -- or 30 gallons or 300 gallons, I can't remember the amount, of fuel. So I suggest to you that that Lizane Malaj is a more reliable witness and the document is a more reliable piece of evidence about who was there at the time those crimes occurred in Korenica and in Meja. Next slide, please. Now, again, the argument is made that there is no plan, but we say when you consider the evidence as a whole it's clear that there was a plan, that General Lazarevic participated in the joint criminal enterprise, and that he should be responsible pursuant to 7(3). I am going to conclude my remarks concerning General Lazarevic and turn the podium over now to Mr. Stamp to talk to you about General Lukic. I'll be back one more time just to sum up on some considerations about evidence, and then we'll be done. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Can I ask you to elucidate something which is bothering my mind. While you were talking -- while you were speaking, you made a reference to the storage of the documents pertaining to the Joint Command in a house or in some place, and then according to yourself this building was destroyed or burnt. Now, can you further elucidate on this with reference to something, and what is your own stand on this and so on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, the evidence, Your Honour, is from the documents and the witnesses. The response to our RFA for documents concerning the Joint Command suggested that the place where those documents might have been stored, those buildings were destroyed. Now, I guess that means, Well, that's probably where the documents were, and since the build was destroyed we can't find them. They may have been kept somewhere else. We don't know. In P1468, I think on the 28th of October, that excerpt we showed you from I think page 163, Mr. Andjelkovic was talking about, Where are we going to keep our documents, and Mr. Sainovic suggested that since they couldn't be kept in the district building - I think that's where the tech headquarters were - that they could be kept in the MUP building. If he's talking about the MUP building in Pristina, we do have evidence that the MUP building in Pristina was bombed in March 1999. So some of the documents that may have remained in Pristina may have been destroyed in that bombing, but other documents that went to President Milosevic's chief of cabinet, we think that's probably Colonel or General Susic who kept the minutes of not only the SDC meetings but also the inter-departmental staff meeting that's in Exhibit P2166. Some Joint Command documents may have been kept there, but -- and I don't recall the evidence about this, and I'm sure my colleagues will call me on this if I'm stating something that's not accurate, but I seem to recall there was some evidence that we had made a request for documents from the military cabinet of President Milosevic and we were told those records no longer existed, that either they had been removed and couldn't be located or that they had been destroyed pursuant to standard procedure after a certain period of time. That's to the best of my recollection, Judge. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, because this is something very important, but I think a lot is being based on assumption. Am I right in thinking that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in the absence of hard documents, sometimes we have to rely on the best inference we can draw from what we do have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're welcome. All right. I'll turn over to Mr. Stamp now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The main thrust that can be discerned, I think, from the closing brief presented on behalf of Mr. Lukic is really that he did not possess any authority over the police in Kosovo, the SUPs, police attached to the SUPs, the special units. He did not have any authority to order or plan or instigate or aid and abet any of them in any of their activities. The submission was made in the brief. Seriously, I believe that the MUP staff was an innocuous police postbox in Kosovo, and they base that submission on the evidence of many former subordinates of Mr. Lukic who testified on his behalf, including Mr. Adamovic, Mr. Mijatovic, Mr. Vucurevic. I discussed some of them yesterday and their credibility and the credibility of these witnesses, so clearly troubling, to say the least, does not make the evidence of any of them in regard to the -- to the authority of the MUP staff any more believable since several of them came to say that it was innocuous, it had -- it was just some people gathering together for meetings but who had no real authority. The main difficulty I think many of these witnesses had, if one reviews the record, is that they could not reconcile their evidence that the MUP staff was powerful -- powerless with the evidence of P1502, the MUP staff mandate issued by the MUP Minister Stojiljkovic in June 1998, and which in almost exact terms was re-issued at the end of May 1999. Nobody could suggest that the minister when he did -- when he issued those declarations, which are fully discussed in the Prosecution's brief, was engaging in an idle project even if he had nothing better to do. But more than that, there are several minutes of the MUP staff meetings, again, discussed in the closing brief, where the chiefs of the SUPs, the commanders of the special units in Kosovo, including the PJP, the SAJ, the JSO, members of the RDB, are present, in attendance, reporting to Lukic and receiving instructions from him. The MUP minutes establish that he in Kosovo along the Prosecution agreed with General Stevanovic when he came down, exercised authority over these commanders and chiefs and, therefore, their respective units and organization.
