And these documents, it is submitted, really speak for themselves. I don't think the authenticity of these documents are in any real question. The Defence spent some time discussing the proposition that there were different structures for the MUP in Kosovo, that the SUPs had their own reporting chain up to the -- to Belgrade, and this was to some degree -- or this was separate from the MUP staff. Your Honours, the Prosecution does not say that the MUP staff abrogated the entire MUP chain in Kosovo. The SUP chiefs still reported to Belgrade, and PJP commanders of units attached to the SUPs still reported to the SUP chiefs, and PJP commanders of the larger PJP units still reported to assistant Minister Stevanovic. However, when they were operational in Kosovo, as the MUP staff mandate, P1505, provides, the MUP staff coordinated them, governed them, and controlled them; and that, it is submitted, is quite clear from the evidence. Thus, there was a dual or parallel chain, and the fact that there is a dual or parallel chain does not mean that one chain, the chain up to Belgrade, has to be excluded necessarily. This dual and parallel chain of authority is borrowed by what Lukic himself said in his OTP interview. He -- and it is -- I commend the interview to Your Honours' review. He accepted that he was responsible for the MUP in Kosovo when they were engaged operationally, and indeed so, it is submitted unequivocally. His interview is P948. In paragraph 13 of the Lukic closing brief, they raise somewhat vaguely challenges about this exhibit. This has been a matter that has been subject to intense litigation in this case over two years, and the Lukic Defence, it is submitted, has not presented anything even slightly credible that the -- that P948, the interview, as it stands now does not accurately reflect the words of Mr. Lukic on any substantive issue. And the Lukic Defence, I don't think, or has not said yet that the formal assistant minister of the police, Lukic, was coerced into making these statements, did not understand what he was saying, or the -- on substantive grounds any of the areas are inaccurate. Many of the statements are dealt with at various places insofar as they are relevant in the Prosecution's closing brief, but some of them, in particular I'd like to highlight as could be seen on the slide before the Court, I should point out that the vast majority of the references can be found in the Prosecution's closing brief from paragraph 211 and from paragraph 1004. Lukic was aware of and understood the scope of the MUP staff mandate, P1505, and further on he said that the task of the task was to coordinate the work of these units, and in this part, these units, the special police units had practically dual responsibility to the commander, that is, the commander of the units or the SUP chiefs, and to the head of the staff, that is to himself. Secondly, he agreed that he had parallel responsibility over the PJP units, which was a main operational unit engaging Kosovo. They had parallel responsibility with Stefanovic and Djordjevic. He was asked at pages 41 to 42, Who had primacy, and he said, In the hierarchy they are by all means above the head of the staff because they are assistant ministers, and this is why I said that the special units had responsibility for the task parallel and together. We had towards it both. He's saying that he as well as the minister had parallel responsibility for the PJP in Kosovo. It is clear from the staff minutes and also accepted by Mr. Lukic in P948 that operational commanders in charge of what was going on in the field would have to report to the MUP in the fulfilment of the tasks. He accepted the role of the Joint Command. He said that as far as the so-called Joint Command is concerned - he referred to it as so-called because as far as I know it has not been officially enacted in any document - "It was called the Joint Command because it was necessary to unite police and army activities and engage the politicians to resolve other issues in Kosovo." And he accepted the work and the meetings of the Joint Command during the indictment period. At page 86 when he was asked about that, he said: "Due to the specific situation during the bombing, the frequent changes of locations of both the corps command and the ministry staff, they met mostly in basements at various locations." And he said finally: "It was most often in the shelter of the Grand Hotel." That is the evidence or part of it. Much more is described in the closing brief, as I indicated, and I don't think there is any point in repeating that here or to elaborate upon it here. In addition to that evidence that is in the brief, there is evidence that is not fully discussed there, the evidence of international representatives who were in Kosovo and who worked with Lukic and who described Mr. Lukic as the most senior MUP person, the person responsible for the MUP in Kosovo. General DZ said that Lukic himself or Lukic introduced himself to him as the Serbian police commander in Kosovo. And he also said or gave examples where in the discussion that he had with General Lukic it was clear that Lukic exercised authority over these forces in Kosovo. Ciaglinski testified to the same effect. He said that when he arrived in Kosovo he was informed that Lukic was the person in charge of the MUP. At the various meetings with the FRY and the KVM commission, Lukic was introduced as the boss of the MUP in Kosovo. He accepted or assumed that Mijatovic worked directly for Lukic because he would always refer or defer to Lukic. And Maisonneauve and Byrnes testified to the same effect that Lukic as far as they were concerned Lukic was the chief of police in Serbia. So from all angles, he had the power, he had the authority to command, to control, and to discipline the forces in Kosovo, the relevant forces in Kosovo. You know, I'm not talking about the traffic police or the other work that police officers do, but those that are operating in the field where the villages are and the towns where the Albanian population was expelled from. All of that evidence is supported by evidence, much of which was dealt with just now by Mr. Hannis. Lukic's presence at various high-level meetings as a representative for the MUP in Kosovo, he was one of the representatives for the MUP at the 21st of July meeting at Beli Dvor in Belgrade where the 1998 summer offensive was planned. He represented the MUP at the Joint Command meetings in 1998 and 1999. He, together with Djordjevic and Stevanovic, was part of the MUP delegation involved in the discussions of the Clark-Naumann Agreement, which included matters impacting the work of the MUP in Kosovo. On the 29th of October, 1998, at the meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Belgrade, he submitted to all the presidents and high-level leaders the report on behalf of the MUP in Kosovo; and if you look at that report, that report covered the MUP operations in all its aspects. And on the 4th of May, he attended a meeting in Milosevic's villa in Belgrade where the leaders of the police and military and the civilian leadership in Serbia were present and provided an overview of the activities of the MUP. I don't think I could elaborate any further usefully on those aspects of the evidence. There are a couple matters that I'd like to refer to which are raised in the brief, and I think I should comment on them. The submission is that Lukic not only was in charge of these operational forces, but he was linked directly to persons involved in the commission of the crimes, and I'll give two examples. We see at paragraph 754 of the closing brief for Mr. Lukic that it is submitted that the sole evidence that Lukic had responsibilities over Trajkovic and the SAJ is in P1505, and there's a reason for this, and that is because Trajkovic was in charge of the SAJ including those persons who committed the Podujevo massacre of the women and children. So there is an attempt to distance Lukic from Trajkovic. Paragraph 1001 of the pre-trial brief discusses P1989, which is a MUP staff meeting on the 4th of April, 1999, where there were several SAJ commanders present, including Trajkovic, and as I said, JSO commanders who were present there reporting to and making proposals to and receiving instructions from Lukic. So Lukic had authority over Trajkovic. As I said, Trajkovic was responsible for the Skorpions, according to the evidence, and is a person who according to Goran Stoparic, the insider police witness who was a member of the Skorpions, in his statement, P2224, he visited the Skorpions shortly after they had murdered all these women and children in Podujevo and thanked them, something that shocked the witness. Trajkovic should have -- well, it is obvious that having regard to what happened at Podujevo, it was obvious to Stoparic and it is obvious to all of us here that Trajkovic 's responsibility would have been to do otherwise in respect to any person that might have been involved in such an incident. The Lukic closing brief suggests that Skorpions were tried, convicted, and sentenced for the crime. True, but this was long after the indictment period, and this occurred in what might have -- might be described as a different era in Serbia, and if one looks at the exhibit referred to, P951, which I think is a document in which they are charged, one will see that the charges later on in Serbia bear little relation to the time in 1999 when Mr. Lukic exercised command responsibility there. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief discusses the evidence of K-83, another police insider who testified about the Suva Reka massacre. I won't discuss further the massacre itself, but one of the points he made in his evidence is that the massacre of the Berisha family was -- the massacre occurred during an operation led by Cegar 1 or Colonel Mitrovic who commanded the 37th PJP Detachment. There has been evidence about Cegar 1 and Colonel Mitrovic. The suggestion at paragraph 895 of the Lukic closing brief that the unit was not involved is not correct. One can check the references to see that it is not correct. The evidence of Stoparic was that this was the unit that led the operation. Colonel Mitrovic was also Lukic's subordinate who reported to him. In P1989, again, at page 2, we see him -- well, the screen is before -- it's interesting to note on this page and I think the previous page and the next page who attended the meetings and gave reports to Mr. Lukic, chiefs of secretariats, and chiefs of PJP detachments who were present there giving reports. And at the bottom of this page we see the said Radoslav Mitrovic, the commander of the 37th Detachment who gave a report to Lukic. And later on in the exhibit, you can see that Lukic issued various directives. So the point is that the -- Lukic had control of the various persons in the field who were involved in the commission of the crimes. He's linked to them as their leader and commander. The Defence argument at paragraph 620 is that General Lukic was not the most senior officer in Kosovo. To some degree, with respect, that is solely non sequitur. What the Prosecution is saying that he was the most senior officer posted in Kosovo, with office in Kosovo. So the minister or the -- or Mr. Djordjevic or Mr. Stevanovic, as the Defence has indicated, they were senior, too, yes, but they were based in Belgrade, and I don't think the Defence has suggested who else was more senior who was down there. I remind the Court that he was a senior police officer, and there are various inferences which Judges I'm sure can infer from the seniority within a disciplined force like the police force or a force intended to be disciplined like the police force. Many inferences as evident, I think, can be drawn, and one is his authority to take steps where he becomes aware that police officers commit crimes, and therefore a distinction must be drawn between what is clear. The Lukic Defence is saying that he was not involved in disciplinary proceedings in the SUPs. Yes, if a policeman didn't come to work on time or was sloppily dressed, that is something that the MUP rules of procedure and the disciplinary procedures in the MUP took care of. That is something for the SUP chief, and that went up to Belgrade. But the most senior police officer in Kosovo who had authority over the operational police in Kosovo had a different responsibility that came to the attention that police officers were involved in murder or ethnic cleansing, looting, his responsibility -- he cannot say that there is a structure in place for that. If we look at the evidence of Bozidar Filic who was asked about -- and he is a SUP chief who testified was asked about that, we can see how -- what I say is a self-evident inference, a self-evident fact, how self-evident it is in the way he dealt with it. This is not something anti-intuitive or non-intuitive. He said the head of the staff -- he agreed that the head of the staff was the most senior officer posted in Kosovo even though more senior officials visited during the war. He said that Lukic did not have direct authority to take measures in case of serious crimes; it was the chief of secretariats. But when pressed about his authority to take direct measures if he knew about crimes, his answer was: "Certainly, certainly. As I said before, there were instructional dispatches on the part of the staff stating that measures should be timely and that both the staff and the ministry need to be advised of the measures taken." So this is an acceptance of what I think is the obvious. Mr. Lukic had responsibility for the conduct of these forces when they were operational and investigated. There is also some direct evidence linking Mr. Lukic to another aspect of the case that I addressed yesterday, and that is evidence linking him to the shipment of the bodies from Serbia -- from Kosovo to Serbia. This is direct evidence from Protic. Protic who said that he knew Lukic before, him and his driver, in 1990 and had spoken to him on the phone before, and he said that he got instructions from General Zekovic, I think it is, in Kosovo -- in Belgrade to go down to Kosovo and to call a number to get instruction as to where to get the bodies from. And when he called the number, the person he spoke to recognised his voice and the manner in which he was addressed, as well. He recognised him to be Mr. Lukic, and he told him where to go and where to get the bodies, and he carried out those instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take you back briefly, Mr. Stamp, to your broad submission that Lukic was in charge of the MUP when they were engaged in action. I maybe have paraphrased what you said. Now, it's easy to understand that submission in relation to PJP units. Can you give an example from the evidence of a situation where the run-of-the-mill police officers in a SUP would be involved in something that would fall under Lukic's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, the run-of-the-mill police officers -- the police officers who were engaged in the field, there are examples, well, many examples discussed in the brief that indicated that they were -- they fell within his responsibilities. When I say "run-of-the-mill," I'm thinking of police officers who were engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your submission was - I've found it now - the SUPs and the PJP reported -- still reported to Belgrade, but when they were operational in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the MUP staff coordinated and controlled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you relate that more specifically to a SUP's activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have the SUP chiefs, and perhaps I could find it in the Prosecution's closing brief. We have the SUP chiefs reporting on the operations to the -- to General Lukic, and we have in those MUP minutes General Stevanovic instructing the SUP chiefs that whenever they have their own plans for anti-terrorist activity they must submit them to the MUP staff first before they could proceed with their own plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's how you fit it into this scheme, that there was, and we've seen -- I think there's more than one example of it, instructions that SUP chiefs have to submit -- or had to devise a plan for anti-terrorist activities and to submit that for approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're talking about the action of any of their staff when engaged in anti-terrorist activity or what is called anti-terrorist activity?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Operational activity in the field is one way one could look at it, and there are in addition to that various directives from General Lukic to the SUP chiefs that they should send reports to him about various activities. These, again, are discussed in the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Protic was a witness, I readily concede, who was involved in criminal activity. Certainly, at least, to knowingly transport and conceal bodies must have been against the law of Serbia. And Your Honours must exercise your own judgement and experience in respect to the testimony of an insider like that who comes and tells you that, I'm telling you the truth, and I was involved in this harvesting, and this is how it occurred. And I agree, I accept that Your Honours have to be very cautious in reviewing evidence of people like that, and in case of this nature we will have people like that, and there will be areas of their testimony which needs to be reviewed, particularly the issue as to his naming General Lukic sometime after he had given his first and second statements to the war crimes investigators in Serbia. Much has been made about it. He explained it. He was cross-examined about it. Those who have experience in dealing with evidence of persons who were involved in the crimes know that many times initially they are very hesitant about naming persons, and at the time in question, at the time when he gave his first statements and took the investigators to Petrovo Selo where he showed them those graves, Mr. Lukic still occupied a position of authority in Serbia. So these are issues which I do not back away from. I accept that that aspect of the evidence must be reviewed carefully, but I commend -- I submit that on a whole his evidence is credible that it was Mr. Lukic that he spoke to and can be relied on by the Tribunal. There are other aspects of the entire testimony that the Court can look to. One of the areas is the testimony of Mr. Kostic and Mr. Furdulovic about Lukic who took over or was appointed to be in charge of the investigations in 2001 and 2002. He ensured, almost to shocking -- almost shockingly that even -- that not even a janitor, as it turned out from the evidence, could be interviewed without him knowing first. These are signs. These are signs that perhaps his engagement may not be as the Defence claimed. What is interesting, again, and a very interesting aspect of the testimony from which I -- I'm sure your experience will draw the appropriate conclusions, is the evidence Sakic, Cedomir Sakic, he the Defence brought to say that, yes, he was engaged to escort Lukic -- sorry, to escort Mr. Protic when Mr. Protic was transporting the bodies from Kosovo to Serbia, and he stuck close to Mr. Protic like glue so Mr. Protic would have never had an opportunity at any time on those trips, some of which lasted over a day; there was one trip when they left Serbia, one they overnighted and then picked up the bodies the next day to carry them back, but he was always so close to Mr. Lukic that Mr. -- Mr. Protic, I beg your pardon, according to him that Mr. Protic would not have had an opportunity to call. That aspect of the evidence where he could not account for four hours of the time when they were supposed to have been together is discussed in the closing brief, but there is another interesting aspect if you look at the extracts before you. You know, he had not seen Mr. Protic for, what is it, five years according to his testimony, and he meets him on the street near to where he lives. At that time, Mr. Protic was running some sort of removal business and was beside his van, and he immediately said -- started speaking against General Lukic, and he said the following words, and this is Basanovic. "I will testify against Mr. Lukic because he did not award me a flat, whereas he had awarded one to the driver Basanovic." Protic was involved in transporting the bodies. Savic was involved in escorting the people who were transporting bodies. I keep -- it's Sakic. Cedomir Sakic was involved in escorting them. The evidence from Protic is that Basanovic who was General Zekovic's driver was also involved in transporting bodies to Kosovo. Now, how after five years could Protic have made such an outburst to Sakic about General Lukic and Basanovic if Sakic did not know that all of them, all of them, were involved in this procedure? There could be no other reason that -- for Protic to be able to say something like that to Sakic. And Sakic was asked why -- why -- he was given an opportunity to explain, why is it that after six years Protic would be telling him about Basanovic and complaining about Lukic if they were not involved, and he couldn't -- well, it's -- I put the answer before the Court. He was given an opportunity to explain and that his answer, it is submitted, that he -- that there is no explanation or no other explanation but that even Sakic knew that this was something that these persons were involved in. Interestingly, a part of the evidence, as well, is that one of the drivers, I think the custodian of Basanovic -- sorry, the custodian of Batajnica who was a protected witness whose acronym I can't recall said that there were at least six trips, and one of the drivers according to Protic of these refrigerated trucks was Radosavljevic, Radosavljevic's driver. Radosavljevic was also a member of the MUP staff of Kosovo. So clearly they were all engaged in this endeavour. We agree with the Defence that Mr. Djordjevic was involved, but there were other senior leadership figures involved. The evidence from K-84 who led the investigations in 2001 when the story came out in the newspapers about these bodies was that when he approached Djordjevic about it, Djordjevic disappeared. They didn't interview Lukic who was the most senior person posted in Kosovo. Lukic was -- Lukic, it is clear, maintained a tight grip on this investigation. This is what Protic said happened when the news broke when it was on the front page of the newspapers in Belgrade every day in 2001. Djordjevic and Lukic discussed with him what should be done with him, and he agreed that he should be transferred, sent outside of Belgrade for the time being, and you will remember he also testified about how he was efficiently retired from the police force during the period of the investigations. So this is a case not of Djordjevic's sole responsibility, but it's another case, it is submitted by the Prosecution, of parallel and dual responsibility. So the Prosecution submits that the evidence has exhaustively discussed in the closing brief and in the other evidence that the Court is aware of which we did not discuss, clearly demonstrates that Mr. Lukic not only was in charge of these forces but had leadership responsibilities to some specific individuals who were involved in these crimes, including scheduled crimes. And with that I will hand over now to Mr. Hannis to wrap up. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to conclude by addressing some general considerations to you regarding how you approach the mountain of evidence that you have to deal with in this case. First of all, there are certain documents that I feel are core documents that will be most helpful to you in understanding the evidence in this case, and I refer them to you for your consideration: The SDC minutes from the Supreme Defence Council; the VJ collegium minutes, they're quite lengthy and sometimes they contain material that may not appear on the surface to be all that helpful or useful to you, but at the same time I think it's useful to you to even go through that because it shows you the relations and the interactions among the individuals involved in the VJ General Staff, the detailed nature of the information they have from all kinds of sources, and I think it's worthwhile for that; the Supreme Command Staff evening briefings during the war will be useful and helpful to you; the Joint Command meetings of 1998 in Exhibit P1468; a body of documents of the VJ and Joint Command decisions and orders and combat reports and post-action analysis by those units engaged in the actions in the field; MUP staff meetings contain a lot of useful information for you; and of course, the suspect interviews. One other group of core documents: The constitutions of the FRY and Serbia, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army, the Law on Internal Affairs, P2166; P1898, the excerpts from Stevanovic's diary; P1011, which was the Markovic document about how the VJ complied with international law; contains a lot of does go documents. One of them I failed to mention earlier when we were talking about the continuation or the existence of the Joint Command is contained in there, and I think Judge Bonomy asked one of the witnesses about that. That's a reference to a Joint Command report dated October 29th about the activities of the Joint Command, and we don't have that document, although apparently it existed, and it's referred to in P1011. P615 is the Kosovo atlas and other maps will be useful to you. In reviewing that evidence, as I've mentioned before, you will find it very helpful to try and do it in a chronological fashion when you can. It gives you context; it will help corroborate other documents and witness testimony; it can assist you in determinations of weight, reliability, and authenticity; and sometimes you will find things that make sense. You will see a meeting, and based on what's said at the meeting if you work backwards you'll say, There should have been some mention of this before or there -- we should see some reflection of this after, and that will help you in evaluating all that evidence. Credibility of witnesses. I've never been in a case this big with this many witnesses, and you've got a lot of witnesses to judge credibility. Now, certainly, you've never been in a case with this many witnesses where you have as many credibility issues as you have in this case. Many witnesses, I say, on both sides were not credible about many issues; however, you as professional Judges, if you find a witness not credible on some answer or answers, you can decide to reject part of their testimony or all of their testimony in light of that, but you have to weigh their evidence in light of all the circumstances. And you as experienced Judges will know those kinds of things that you need to factor in in making that determination. Some direct conflicts in the evidence of witnesses are going to have to be resolved where, for example, we had VJ insiders or MUP insiders and their commanders or their colleagues came in and said something that was 180 degrees opposite. You're going to have to resolve some of those conflicts and consider the bias, the motive of the people testifying, consider when they first made their statements, how they may have changed over time. Sometimes you had several witnesses come in and talk about an event, a document, an institution. In my experience in dealing with witnesses, even in a simple case like a car crash or a bank robbery, you may have five witnesses who were there at the same time, and you would expect them to report basically the same thing. But it's human nature and it's funny how you will get some widely disparate reports about the same thing. But with the other information you have, you're often able to sort through who got it right, who got it wrong, and why they got it wrong. But the opposite side of the coin, though, however, sometimes you may have eye-witnesses who come in and tell exactly the same story. That should cause suspicion on your part, I suggest, based on my experience with human nature because that may suggest that people have decided, Oh, we have to tell this story a certain way because otherwise it will look bad for us. Sometimes too much consistency can be a bad thing. I ask you to bear that in mind in evaluating this evidence. You're going to have to consider the testimony of some of the Prosecution insider witnesses like K-25, K-54, K-82, K-89 compared to the testimony of VJ and MUP commanders Delic, Vukovic, et cetera. You're going to have to consider Peraj versus Lazarevic and Kotur and make a decision about who you believe and why. This relates to circumstantial evidence. As I said earlier on, this is not a case where we have a confession. We don't have a smoking-gun document. We don't have a copy of the plan to expel Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo, but, again, I think in the experience of human nature we oftentimes find that circumstantial evidence can be more compelling and more trustworthy sometimes than a confession or a document. In deciding whether it's the only reasonable inference to be drawn that there was a plan, it should be viewed in the totality of the circumstances, not in an isolated fashion. I think it was in General Ojdanic's brief where there was a good job of taking individual aspects of the whole thing and offering an alternative explanation for each, which on the surface has appeal and looks good, but that's too simple, I suggest to you. Occam's razor is a principle that you're probably familiar with if things are subject to more than one reasonable explanation. Oftentimes the simple one is the correct one. I'd like to give you an analogy based on my early days as a prosecutor in a drunk driving case, and I don't mean the demean these proceedings or the seriousness of the kinds of crimes we're talking about here, but the process is the same; the analysis is the same, and I'll give you an example. A highway patrolman stops a driver because his driving is erratic, speed is fast, slow, its up, it's down, he's weaving in the roadway. He talks to the driver. He smells what appears to be alcohol on his breath. He has bloodshot and watery eyes and a red nose. His speech is slurred. He gives him some field sobriety test, walk in a straight line, he can't do, trying to close his eyes and lean his head back and touch his finger to his nose. He misses badly. There are beer cans on the floor board in the car. The case goes to trial, and the defendant comes in, and he has an explanation for every one of those things. The bad driving, the weaving, and the inconsistent speed was I had a mechanical problem with my car. You know, the suspension was bad and the accelerator was messed up. The alcohol on my breath, that was the Breathalyzer -- not the Breathalyzer. That was the breath freshener I used because I was on my way to see my girlfriend, and there's some alcohol in that. The red nose, I have allergies. Bloodshot and water eyes, I was out working in the field all day. Slurred speech, I bit my tongue accidentally when I saw your red light in my rearview mirror, and I was nervous. The field sobriety test, I couldn't walk a straight line because I had on my new boots and they hurt my feet. My finger to the nose, I still had the lingering effects of an inner ear infection after my last flight and it affected my balance when I closed my eyes. The beer cans on the floor board were left there by a hitchhiker I had picked up and dropped off shortly before you stopped me, officer. All reasonable explanations, all possible. But is it more likely that those ten different varying explanations serendipitously came together in one place at one time, or is the more likely explanation he was drunk, he was driving drunk? We say you can make an analogy in this case, but on top of that, in this case, throw in the testimony of the survivors of the massacres and the deportations. In my drunk driving case that would be like, I found the bartender and the waitress who came in and said, yeah, he was here. He had four beers before he left ten minutes before you stopped him. Consider all that evidence together, and we say the circumstantial evidence leads to only one reasonable conclusion. And that's where we hope you will as the professional Judges take your common sense with you when you sit down to consider the evidence in this case. As you said, Mr. President, I think on at least one occasion, maybe more, if it's called a cat and it looks like a cat, it's probably a cat. I think you told Professor Markovic calling it a dog does not change the nature of the cat. Where I came from, we used to say if it looks like a duck and it walks like a duck and it quacks like a duck, it's probably a duck. Same principle, Your Honour, and we ask you to bear that in mind when it comes time to write your judgement. My last remark does relate to sentencing. In the event that you find one or more of these accused guilty of any of the crimes charged, you're going to have to impose sentence. The general considerations are in Rules 101 of our Rules of Procedure and Article 24 of the Statute. We have recommended a range of 20 years to life to be given out as you deem fit for any accused that you might convict, and I only point to you the aggravating factors that we think you should consider in the event you are going to impose sentence on one or more of the accused, and those are the leadership roles that these individuals had, the vulnerability of the particular victims in this case, and the victim impact, including the duration of the harm. For many of those people, that harm is permanent. Some of them are dead. Those who survived will probably never be the same as a result of what they experienced, as a result of the commission of these crimes. And with that, Your Honour, that concludes my remarks. I only want to thank you for the opportunity to have addressed you and to tell you it's been a professional honour and pleasure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would probably suit everyone, I suspect, Mr. O'Sullivan, if we adjourn now and resumed at a quarter to 2.00 when we can hear your submission or a large part of it without interruption. So we'll adjourn now until quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, your submissions on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon to you and the Trial Chamber, and good afternoon to my learned friends from the Office of the Prosecutor. At the outset, we have to say that we are prepared to concede based on the Prosecution's review of the evidence that they could prove the guilt of the drunk driver, but we make no further concessions. On a more serious note, Your Honour, the Chamber has had the opportunity to review Mr. Milutinovic's final brief and his prayer for full acquittal. I will not recite the contents of our brief, but I will respond to the Prosecution's submissions that demonstrate to you that the Prosecution has utterly failed to prove the case against Mr. Milutinovic and that you should acquit him. I'd like to begin with the allegations made by the Prosecutor that in 1998 and 1999 that Mr. Milutinovic obstructed and derailed the negotiating process and that he destroyed the possibility of bringing about a peaceful resolution of the Kosovo crisis, and that this created a window of opportunity for the members of the JCE to carry out their plan. The Prosecution says this is evidence of criminal intent and criminal conduct, proof of a JCE and proof of Mr. Milutinovic's participation in the commission of a JCE. Now, yesterday the Prosecutor said that they've presented comprehensive and conclusive evidence to you. Now, we must say with all due respect to the Prosecutor that based on the evidence in this case we find that the allegations and the submissions of the Prosecutor are nothing short of astounding. They are astoundingly incomplete, astoundingly incorrect, and misguided. All of us who sat through this trial for two years, we saw tens of exhibits, numerous witnesses concerning the legitimate and serious attempts made by Mr. Milutinovic and others in 1998 and 1999 to find a viable, lasting, and fair agreement to bring about peace in Kosovo and Metohija. We saw and heard from international players, Kosovar Albanians, federal and republican politicians, and here I'm thinking about John Crosland, the British military attache, Ambassador Petritsch, Veton Surroi, Momir Bulatovic, Zivadin Jovanovic, Ratko Markovic to name a few. And we've heard that powerful members of the international community supported the separatist aspirations of the KLA, turned a blind eye to KLA activities, and made secret deals with the Kosovar Albanians on independence, while at the same time casting public blame on the Serbs for failure of the process as a pretext to bomb the FRY. The OTP knows this is the evidence. We all know that this is the evidence, yet the Prosecutor continues to allege that Mr. Milutinovic acted criminally. There's a flagrant disregard for the evidence. The Prosecution ignores the evidence that we set out in our final brief at paragraphs 127 to 182 concerning 1998, and I must review this with you because there's a complete disregard by the Prosecutor for this evidence. We know that as early as the 10th of March, 1998, the Government of the Republic of Serbia created a delegation to negotiate self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija. And on the 18th of March, Mr. Milutinovic made a declaration where he held himself out as the guarantor for the process. Now, yesterday at page 26820, my learned friend says that it's unclear what it meant to be the guarantor or questions what it means to be a guarantor, but Professor Markovic at page 13133 said that it was Mr. Milutinovic's personal commitment to the peace process, that he represented the state of Serbia and symbolised its unity as the president of the republic, and that he was speaking in that capacity. The negotiations were of a political nature and representatives of the government and the leaders of the Kosovar Albanians were expected to negotiate. There was no other state organ involved. And Mr. Milutinovic, as we will see as I review this evidence, used his experience as a politician, as a diplomat, and his role as the -- or his function as the president of the republic using best attempts to make that happen. Now, we know that in early March or by late March, the 23rd of March, we had the education agreement, and steps were taken despite very difficult circumstances for the remainder of 1998 up to and including the 28th of March, 1999, after the commencement of the war, to fulfil the education agreement, hand over institutions, repair buildings, get supplies up and running. We have evidence of that, and Mr. Milutinovic supported the initiative. The evidence is that he expressed to those around him that he wanted an agreement on education at all costs, and there's the evidence of the letter he received from Monsignor Palija of the San Egidio community in June; and as soon as Mr. Milutinovic received the letter, he forwarded the letter to those who were responsible for implementation, to move faster, to make sure it got done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: By the end of March -- by the end of March 1998, the state delegation was expanded to include the national minority and ethnic communities of Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. O'Sullivan not knock on the desk, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- in the National Assembly. The delegation included the national minorities and ethnic communities in Kosovo, the full spectrum of political representatives, and the Special Envoy to the federal president who is Mr. -- Dr. Kutlesic, deputy federal prime minister. On that same day, 31st of March, the UN Security Council Resolution 1160 said this: It welcomed the statement Mr. Milutinovic had made on the 18th of March; it welcomed the signing of the implementation of the education agreement; it called for immediate dialogue to begin on substantial autonomy, through peaceful means, without precondition, and based on the territorial integrity of the FRY and international standards such as the UN charter, the Helsinki Final Act, and OSCE standards. And those are precisely the same parameters that Mr. Milutinovic advocated on the 18th of March in his declaration. Now, in 1998 Mr. Milutinovic was in Kosovo five times. On four occasions he accompanied the state delegation to meetings. The fifth time was in September when he was in Kosovo following the killing of civilians by the KLA at Radonjic Lake where he laid a wreath and toured the area. The most noteworthy visits he made were on the 18th and 25th of November, 1998, when he accompanied the state delegation. By this time we've had months of shuttle diplomacy which began in July under the auspices of Ambassador Hill, who was US ambassador to Macedonia; Ambassador Petritsch, who was the Austrian ambassador to the FRY; and the EU Special Envoy for Kosovo. The Chamber has the evidence of the 15 draft agreements that were prepared in Mr. Milutinovic's office by his staff. Mr. Kojic testified about that. Mr. Kojic told you that Professor Markovic and Professor Kutlesic were engaged with Ambassador Hill and Jim O'Brien from the US State Department. In the same period, Mr. Milutinovic was meeting with Ambassador Hill and the two members of the state delegation I just mentioned in an attempt to move the process forward through shuttle diplomacy. Now, in relation to the meeting on the 18th in Pristina, four days earlier Mr. Milutinovic had sent letters of invitation to Dr. Rugova, representatives of the ethnic minorities in Kosovo, Ambassador Petritsch, and ambassadors for three of the permanent members of the UN Security Council, the US, Russia, and China. And when he was in Pristina that day, he made remarks at the beginning and at the end of the meeting, and we've included those in our brief in annex 3 and 4. But in his remarks, Mr. Milutinovic stressed for peaceful co-existence in Kosovo and Metohija and common life together, free of conflict, xenophobia, chauvinism, or religious or historical prejudice, and he advocated modern democratic solutions to solve the problem: self-governance, parliamentary system with an executive and judiciary, local police, direct multi-party elections, multi-ethnic and a multi-confessional society. And he concluded by repeating and emphasizing his personal commitment to the process, and he also expressed his disappointment in that the representatives of the leading political parties of the Kosovar Albanians have not responded to invitations that had come out, and I'll come back to how many there were. But he remained open and hopeful that they would engage. That's on the 18th of November. Now, between the -- that meeting and the second meeting I'd like to talk about on the 25th, Mr. Milutinovic took a number of initiatives to move -- to attempt to move the process forward. On the 19th, the day after the Pristina meeting, he met the political representatives from Kosovo who were there back in Belgrade. He sent letters of invitation to Mr. Qosja, Mr. Hyseni, and Mr. Demaqi. On the 20th of November, the day after, he held separate meetings; Mr. Milutinovic held separate meetings in Belgrade with federal and republican politicians from the full spectrum of the political galaxy of Serbia and the FRY including opposition parties. That same day, a joint proposal on the political framework of self-governance in Kosovo was discussed. Mr. Milutinovic called for a continuation of talks on the 25th in Pristina. Letters of invitation were again sent out to Dr. Rugova and others. I take you to the 23rd of November where, again, Mr. Milutinovic is meeting with Ambassador Hill, Dr. Markovic, and Dr. Kutlesic, where they reviewed the events of the previous days in Pristina, the meetings in Belgrade, the joint proposal, and how the joint proposal itself could be the main pillar of a political solution within the framework of the FRY and Serbia according to international standards. Well, on the 25th of November the joint proposal was signed in Pristina accompanied by a document that has become known as the Pristina declaration. It was signed by Dr. Markovic on behalf of the Republic of Serbia, Dr. Kutlesic on behalf of the FRY, and the representatives of the national and political parties. Well, Dr. Rugova did not attend. Now, as a parenthesis, we do have Exhibit 6D1671 which is a Rule 70 Exhibit which I will not go into any detail on because it's Rule 70, but the Chamber can look at it. But the document does tell us -- I won't mention the source. The document does tell us that by that time members of Dr. Rugova's party had been arrested by the secret police of the KLA and they were going to stand trial under the KLA's system. Now, the process did not end on the 25th of November because the evidence is, on the 2nd of December, Ambassador Hill came back with a further draft, and the evidence is this -- this draft presented by Ambassador Hill through the shuttle diplomacy was acceptable to the Serbian side. Now, despite that, the Prosecution cites in its brief the testimony of Ambassador Petritsch and claims that his evidence shows a lack of sincerity from the Serbian side, that they refused international mediation, that the Serbs hindered international mediation, and that they refused to meet with the Kosovar Albanian leadership. I invite you to look at what Ambassador Petritsch actually said. Ambassador Petritsch's testimony is this: He welcomed the three-plus-three agreement. It was consistent with Resolution 1160. It was a positive step. He considered the Yeltsin-Milosevic agreement of mid-June as a very positive step forward, a significant compromise by FRY and Serbia, a compromise to internationalise the process. He called it an historic declaration, and we know that that agreement brought in KDOM. It allowed for freedom of movement of diplomats and humanitarian organizations. It provided for state assistance through the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija and, also, a further undertaking to bring in and negotiate with the OSCE of monitoring. The Milosevic-Yeltsin agreement also signalled the beginning of the shuttle diplomacy I've just mentioned, which was -- involved Ambassadors Hill and Petritsch. But Ambassador Petritsch says more. He considered the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement of October 1998 as an important next step of the involvement of the international community as well as all the subsequent agreements that flowed from that with OSCE, KVM, NATO, and KDOM. Ambassador Petritsch considered the joint proposal of the 20th of November and the Pristina declaration of 25 November as a demonstration of the commitment of the Serbian side to fulfil the timetable which the Serbian government had set for itself in its 11-point framework on the 13th of October, 1998. The Prosecution cites at paragraph 250 of its brief this, the evidence of Mr. Petritsch, Ambassador Petritsch, that on the 11th of March, 1998, an invitation was sent from the state delegation to the Albanian leadership one day after the creation of the state delegation, and that that was short notice and that was a sign of bad faith. Well, fair enough. It was short notice. It was the first day after the creation of the delegation. But what does Ambassador Petritsch tell us? He says that repeated efforts were made to encourage all Kosovar Albanian representatives to meet. He knew himself of 12 to 15 invitations that were destined to encourage dialogue, and Professor -- Ambassador Petritsch said there could be no legitimate reason for one side to refuse 15 invitations, and he knew that Mr. Milutinovic was constantly emphasizing his personal commitment to the process and the importance of finding a resolution to the problem in Kosovo and Metohija. Now, that's only the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch that I've been referring to in this last segment. There's a wealth of evidence from other individuals and other sources in this case. And what of the claim by the Prosecution that the state delegation refused to meet with the Kosovar Albanians? Let's put the shoe on the right foot. In 1998 and at Rambouillet and Paris, it was the state delegation that always requested, all encouraged face-to-face talks, and it was always the Albanian side which refused and which was supported in not sitting down with the state delegation. At paragraph 588 of the Prosecutor's brief, they make reference to a letter by Dr. Qosja and Mr. Hyseni. It's a response, I say. It's a response to the letter Mr. Milutinovic sent inviting them, and their response is that meetings were improvised and the discussions were hasty. Now, we're in November 1998. We know that there's been shuttle diplomacy through Ambassador Hill. The UN Security Council by this time has twice called for urgent and immediate negotiations. That's on the 31st of March in the 1160 and the 23 September in 1199. There was also a timetable requested by the UN Security Council and a process that it would include all ethnic nations in Kosovo, and only -- we know that only representatives of the leading political parties refused to participate -- the representatives of the leading Albanian parties refused to participate. In that same paragraph, 588, Prosecution refers to the letter from Mr. Demaqi, his response to Mr. Milutinovic. That's 1D92. We invite you to look at our brief at paragraph 153 because the essence of Mr. Demaqi's response is that it was not clear to him whether Mr. Milutinovic was inviting him as a private citizen or as the chief political representative of the KLA. But what's the evidence in relation to this letter? Well, it's P604. That's Prosecution Exhibit P604, which is Mr. Milutinovic's interview with the Prosecutor. It's Mr. Milutinovic who provided this letter to the Prosecutor, and he told them that Demaqi was insincere in this letter because clearly, Mr. Milutinovic said, he'd invited him as a representative of the KLA, just as he had invited Mr. Rugova, Mr. Qosja, and Mr. Hyseni in their official capacities as representatives of the leading Kosovar Albanian political parties. And to round off 1998, we have the evidence of the press conference given by Mr. Demaqi on the 8th of December, 1998. This is a week after the final Hill proposal on the 2nd of December, which, again, P604 tells us, Mr. Milutinovic told the Prosecutor, that on the 2nd of December both the Americans and the Serbs were in general agreement with that proposal. But Demaqi from the KLA denounces the Hill proposal as utterly unacceptable, and he repeats his historic -- what he considers to be his historic mission, which is the unification of Albanians across Albania, Kosovo, and Macedonia, and we've heard evidence from Mr. Petritsch and Momir Bulatovic about the notion of greater Albania. And this letter also reveals that Mr. Agani had not made any real proposals. It was a question by the Presiding Judge during the testimony of Ambassador Petritsch which reveals that. So clearly, in 1998 there can be no basis for alleging a lack of sincerity or refusing international mediation, certainly no criminal intent, and no criminal conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, just a point of detail. Is there any evidence of what happened between the 25th of November and the 2nd of December to create the final draft? You've referred to some evidence there of the KLA response to Serb acceptance of it. Do we know how the situation changed from being a document which only minority parties were involved in to a proposal in a different form?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the proposal was a result of efforts made by the state delegation at late November in Pristina, and the 2nd of December document is a document issued by Ambassador Hill, who was doing the shuttling. So it was the final Hill version, and you remember that Mr. Kojic had been preparing these drafts and they'd been shuttled between the state delegation and Ambassador Hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is there any evidence of who Hill met and discussed matters with between the 25th and the 2nd, or is there just a vacuum?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, there's no details on who he met, but he and Ambassador Petritsch were doing the shuttling between the state delegation and Kosovar Albanians. They'd been doing that since July so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any evidence in the case, though, of who these Kosovar Albanians were?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, obviously the -- Mr. Demaqi and Mr. Agani [Realtime transcript read in error, "again"], Hyseni had been receiving that. They responded to this in their press release, the press release on the 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I move now to 1999 on the same theme, and I must begin by correcting what we say are some factual errors in paragraph 252 of the Prosecutor's brief. This is in relation to Rambouillet. At paragraph 252, the Prosecutor states that at Rambouillet the parties would refine the draft proposals presented earlier by Hill, Petritsch, and Mayorski, and that the Rambouillet was a continuation of negotiations conducted by the Contact Group in 1998. Well, just as a background matter, that's incorrect. The Contact Group was not involved in the 1998 process. The shuttle diplomacy was between -- under the auspices of Ambassador Hill. It was, as I said, the American ambassador to Macedonia and Ambassador Petritsch who was the Austrian ambassador to the FRY and Special Envoy to the EU for Kosovo. Ambassador Mayorski only became involved at Rambouillet as the Russian representative, and it's also incorrect to say that there had been an earlier draft presented to the parties at Rambouillet because as Ambassador Petritsch told us, the Rambouillet document, as we've seen, the Rambouillet document was presented piecemeal at Rambouillet over a two-week period, and Ambassador Petritsch told us that negotiations among the six Contact Group countries took up more time than shuttling between the two delegations. Now, in our brief at paragraphs 183 and 244, we present a full and complete presentation of the evidence concerning Rambouillet, and it's our position that Mr. Milutinovic and the state delegation did not obstruct, derail, or in any way destroy the possibility of bringing about a peaceful resolution in France. What do we know? Well, we know that on the 4th of February, 1999, the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia responded positively to the Contact Group invitation, established a delegation of experts and experienced members, gave them a mandate based on the ten non-negotiable principles of the Contact Group. It included representatives from the FRY. We know that there was a joint federal platform supporting this delegation. It was by and large the same individuals who had been negotiating in -- or attempting to negotiate in 1998 who were aware of the situation in Kosovo, aware of the law, and aware of life in that part of the Republic of Serbia. As we know, the Rambouillet process lasted from the 6th of February until the 23rd of February, initially planned for one week. Now, within that first week, what did the state delegation do? Well, they requested the full text as soon as they arrived in France. They requested face-to-face meetings with the Kosovar Albanians. They requested the two parties as a sign of good faith sign the ten non-negotiable principles of the Contact Group, and at that point, the co-chairs, Mr. Vedrine and Mr. Cook, assured the state delegation that there was no need to sign the ten non-negotiable principles and that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY and Serbia was assured. And lastly, at the end of that first week, on Friday the 12th, the delegation renewed its request to receive the full text that was being offered at Rambouillet. Now, by the second week, the state delegation had been given what was considered to be the full political components of the accord. Ambassador Petritsch told us that by the end of that week, the 19th and the 20th, that's the Friday night, they worked -- he worked from 7.00 p.m. until 5.00 the next morning along with Dr. Markovic and others to make significant progress on the precise terms of the political components of the agreement. It was that next day, the 20th, the second Saturday -- end of the second week where Mr. Milutinovic accompanied the state delegation and told the Contact Group foreign ministers that there was general agreement on their side as to the political components of the Rambouillet agreement. Mr. Milutinovic had arrived at the end of the first week because initially it was supposed to be a one-week get-together, and the evidence from Mr. Petritsch and from Mr. Markovic is that Mr. Milutinovic had the same relationship with the delegation in 1999, in Rambouillet, as he had had in 1998 as the guarantor of the process. He was not there as someone's mouthpiece; he was not there as someone to obstruct. Now, that's what the state delegation -- that's their -- that was their position by the end of the second week at Rambouillet. During that same period, Veton Surroi told us that by the 18th - that's Thursday - the Kosovar Albanian delegation had rejected the agreement. They said it was unacceptable because it referred to the sovereignty of the FRY, that authority originated according to the agreement in the FRY, powers were derived from the FRY, and there was no reference to a referendum. Mr. Surroi told us, and Mr. Surroi, of course, was a member of this delegation, that other members of the delegation would not touch the document and they wanted to quit. And when the Kosovar representatives came before the first ministers -- the foreign ministers of the Contact Group on Saturday, they rejected it. Mr. Thaqi told Mr. Dini when asked, It doesn't have a referendum; it's unacceptable. And that's when Mr. Dini turned to Mrs. Albright and said, See, I told you so, and she took off her headphones in exasperation, apparently. And Mr. Cook said, Something's missing which is non-negotiable, and the meeting was adjourned. Now, let's recall that two days prior to this meeting with the Contact Group foreign ministers, that is the 18th, there had been a secret meeting between General Clark and KLA members of the Kosovar Albanian delegation outside the castle, and there General Clark was discussing what would become chapters 2, 5, and 7 of the Rambouillet agreement. But by this time, these chapters had not been discussed in the Contact Group, had not been approved by the Contact Group, and certainly they had not been tabled at Rambouillet. These chapters, in particular chapter 7, was prepared by NATO, and the evidence is that General Clark was trying to convince the KLA to accept the agreement and that these chapters 2, 5, and 7 would eventually be included at a later date. So by the 20th of February, we have a situation where the Contact Group foreign ministers have been told by the state delegation and Mr. Milutinovic as their chaperon that the political components of the Rambouillet document are acceptable, generally acceptable; and the KLA has told the Contact Group foreign ministers that they rejected it, that between the 20th and the 23rd, the last three days, a series of events unfolded which we say were planned by Mrs. Albright and implemented by people like Mr. Hill, Petritsch, and others. And the purpose of this was to find a way to start bombing the FRY. We know that by this point Mrs. Albright had told Veton Surroi and Mr. Thaqi, and it was known by Ambassador Petritsch as well. She said if the Kosovars sign and the Serbs do not, then NATO will bomb the FRY. Privately, she was reprimanding Mr. Thaqi for not being a leader, for not agreeing to the political components because otherwise, if he didn't do that, NATO couldn't engage; while at the same time, publicly she's blaming the Serbs for failure on the 20th. Now, the events that unfolded over the next three days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is evidence of that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what form? That at that point in time, after the Serbs have said they'll agree, that she is publicly saying that they won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's -- it's in one of our annexes. I think I can find it for you. Your Honour, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be answered this minute. No, it would help to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because I just have a feeling there's another vacuum in here, as well, about just exactly -- it's a big leap that you've suggested we take, and it may be that what you're about to say does fill what appears to me to be a vacuum, but you're saying that as of this time a strategy has developed, a joint criminal enterprise on the part of the international politicians to create a situation to justify bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll find the reference. It's a clip that was shown to Ambassador Petritsch in annex 9 of our brief. That's Exhibit 1D205. It was originally a Prosecution exhibit, 771. That's where we have Mrs. Albright speaking and Mr. Thaqi speaking, and in addition to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the Fall of Milosevic, again, is it, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That corroborates what Ambassador Petritsch and what Mr. Surroi said, and it corroborates the fact when we get into the secret side letters it follows that that's exactly what happened in Rambouillet, that Mrs. Albright needed the pretext of the Serbs being the bad guys so, as her spokesman said, the world would know whose side to be on, and that's a statement he made publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have to bear in mind that this is a documentary film compiled after the event and it may record words, but the question is the order of events at the moment, and does it help us with the order of these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it helps corroborate the events as they were told by you by participants, particularly Mr. Surroi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and Ambassador Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What is important to understand these events are the attempts by Mrs. Albright through a side arrangement with the Kosovar Albanians to accept the political components of Rambouillet, which by this point they'd rejected by the 20th. Now, this is all set out in our brief, but I'll slowly review it. There are in fact two side letters. The first one is from the 21st of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we're quite clear about these, Mr. O'Sullivan. It's your suggestion that this is all designed from that point on as a pretext to justify bombing. And that's a very strong allegation to make, and it's the evidence for that that I'm anxious to find. I mean, you can't just deduce that from the side letters --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that is one thing conclude that the Serbs were not being told the whole story about the US position on this, but quite another to say that this is designed to justify bombing. If you do things secretly and keep the information from the Serbs, it's not likely to influence their behaviour, whereas if you tell them something that is plainly unfair, then I can see that you might be trying to set up a situation where you might bomb them. But that's a difficult argument to follow if you're basing it on secret material.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In our brief we fully set out what we say the strategy was, and the strategy was that the Americans in particular were convinced that the Albanians and the Serbs would accept the political components on the 20th, and the Serbs did, and the Albanians wouldn't. And with that in place, chapters 2, 5, and 7 were going to be presented as a fait accompli, which -- and chapter 7 in particular was problematic for a number of reasons. It wasn't approved or discussed in the Contact Group. It provided for free -- basically free -- the occupation if NATO determined of the FRY to move about freely and without any questions asked. And it's the totality of these events, and the secrecy is important because Ambassador Petritsch says at one point that he distanced himself from the second side letter. The first one was vetoed by the EU, by Russia, and it certainly would have been unacceptable to the Serbs. And at 9.00 in the morning on the 23rd, the last day, is where the first time that chapters 2, 5, and 7 are tabled. The Serbian side knew that the -- those chapters had not been approved by the Contact Group. Ambassador Mayorski told them so. Now, they're there invited by the Contact Group, and a member of the Contact Group, an important country in the Contact Group, a permanent member of the Security Council, says to them, This isn't part of the agreement or it hasn't been approved, and they're quite at liberty to ask what's been going on here, while at the same time they're being demonised in the process as being the people who are responsible for the failure two days earlier when in fact there is no failure from their side. And the events of the 23rd are revealing. The delegation's asked by 1.00 in the afternoon, some two and a half hours later, to give its views on the agreement, and they comply. They comply. They comply with the letter at 1.00 sharp, but they point out that more room is necessary, that more negotiation is necessary on the outstanding issues, the fine-tuning, but importantly on the political components because they were not reconciled with the FRY and Serbian constitutional and legal framework, issues like the constitution, the president of Kosovo and Metohija, the constitutional court, property. That's all set out in the first letter sent by the delegation. Now, Professor Markovic pointed out that the problem was that you had Anglo-Saxon lawyers making proposals in these agreements that didn't fit in with the continental FRY constitutional legal framework. The general principles were acceptable; the details had to be flushed out, and they made that clear on the 23rd, the Serb delegation. And they wrote to the Contact Group and they said this, two things. All elements of self-government at the time of defining the agreement have to be known and clearly defined. In further work, this should be adequately addressed and consistently resolved. And the second point that they made to the Contact Group is that the FRY agreed to discuss the scope and character of international presence in Kosmet to implement the agreement to be accepted in Rambouillet, so an undertaking to refine the political components and to discuss implementation. Now, that same day, the last day of the conference, Mr. Surroi told us that the -- that Albanian delegation which had rejected the political component had stopped working, just sitting around having lunch, wasting time, he said. Now, by this time we know that Mr. Thaqi is working to kill the Rambouillet agreement. And then we have what occurs in the Kosovar delegation room, and it's not something you can make up because it's nothing short of absurd, where Chris Hill shows up dishevelled and says, Okay, guys, we've got five minutes, are you going to sign this thing? And they come up with the idea of having a letter from the Kosovars to Mrs. Albright, a mirror image of the letter that has been vetoed by the EU [Realtime transcript read in error, "Security Council"] and Russia. And they type this up on the computer and people from the state department block Mr. Thaqi's access to the computer like in a basketball game, to quote Mr. Surroi. And the letter is taken from there directly to Mrs. Albright, and that's when her spokesman James Rubin goes public and says, The Albanians have chosen peace, the Serbs have not, and now there's the clarity the world needed in deciding whose side they should be on. Now, this side letter remains secret.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly requested to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- whether he knew about any side letters, side deals, arrangements that weren't tabled that the parties didn't know about, and he said, no, he didn't know about that. And then when he was shown the letter that I've just described, the one that was signed by Mr. Surroi, he tried to distance himself from it. He said, well, that's -- that was a side letter between the Americans and the Kosovars, not between the Contact Group and the Kosovars, but of course, Ambassador Hill is one of the three negotiators for the Contact Group. Now, why would Ambassador Petritsch be reluctant to admit to this letter and then distance himself from it? Well, he was aware of the US strategy of having -- finding a way to get the Albanians to agree, to cast blame on failure of talks on Serbia. He was aware that the cover letter of the 23rd of February, the one in closing chapters 2, 5, and 7 have not been signed by Ambassador Mayorski, had not been approved by the Contact Group. What he did not know, however, in this courtroom was that that letter had become public, and it became public because it was published in a book by Professor Weller, that's 1D18, and Professor Weller was an advisor to the Kosovar Albanians. So Ambassador Petritsch was caught out. The ambassador had no clothes. And what else do we know from Ambassador Petritsch's testimony? We know that on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the speaker is kindly requested to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and we have to say the ambassador had no clothes. The other thing we know from Ambassador Petritsch is that he and Ambassador Hill on the last day of Rambouillet are working with the Albanians in drafting a public statement from the Albanian delegation, and he and Ambassador Hill are advising the Kosovars to put in their statement that after three years there will be a referendum in Kosovo on independence. Now, before he was caught out Ambassador Petritsch was telling you that a referendum was a terrible idea in the Balkans. It leads to war in Bosnia, couldn't have such a thing, and yet his own internal memo to his foreign ministry in Austria is saying that he and Ambassador Hill are advising the Kosovars to do just that, and what is perceived as a unilateral declaration by the Kosovars is in fact supported by the secret letter to Mrs. Albright with the collaboration of two of the three negotiators, Ambassador Hill and Ambassador Petritsch. Now, in the periods between Rambouillet and Paris --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you just hold on a second, please, Mr. O'Sullivan. There is evidence which I think came from Mr. Bulatovic that by the 18th of February the Serbian government -- sorry, the FRY government had a position on the military annex, these chapters 2, 5, and 7. They clearly -- well, on one view of that evidence, by the 18th of February, they knew about the existence of these. Now, the particular exhibit is 2D221. Do you have any comment to make on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe there is an exhibit that says just the opposite that was sent to the federal government, that's referred to in our brief. Indeed, on the 19th a telex was sent to the federal government saying there is no -- they know of no military annex. That's in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does your -- remind me, does your brief deal with Bulatovic's own evidence on this, where he said that it was a diplomatic response to the military annex offered to the negotiators in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Bulatovic or Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, in Bulatovic's evidence at 13847.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My colleagues are telling me that it's Zivadin Jovanovic, the foreign minister, not the prime minister Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 17th of August, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the reference I have -- the exhibit I have is in paragraph 205 of our brief. It's Exhibit 2D211, and the FRY ministry -- Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported to the federal government on the 19th that the state delegation had not received any military annex with similar proposals at Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's a document that was shown to Foreign Minister Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just give me -- the reference I'm about to make is to the evidence of Bulatovic, and it's at 13847, where he says: "It was sent to the federal prime minister and the cabinet by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs asking that the position of the foreign ministry be discussed and that if they're adopted they should become the standpoints of the federal government. This is a diplomatic response of our ministry to the military annex offered to the negotiators in Rambouillet."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's exactly what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which suggests that by the 18th of February -- actually, the English is the 19th, but the original says the 18th of February of the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Point 1 is what I just quoted to you. Point 1 of that document says: "Our delegation did not receive any military annex or similar military proposals at Rambouillet." And paragraph 2 says what I've been saying, Contact Group did not discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say about Bulatovic's evidence, is my question. Is he wrong, or is he lying or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't see a problem with what Bulatovic said. They received this document saying there is no -- they had not received a military annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the evidence of Professor Markovic is that it was presented for the first time at 9.00 in the morning on the 23rd of February, the last day. Well, in the period between Rambouillet and Paris, the Prosecution alleges that there was a complete change of attitude towards the Rambouillet agreement, then, that Milutinovic made a statement to that effect. That's at paragraph 226 of the Prosecutor's brief, and that's untrue. Ambassador Petritsch is the source of that claim, but what you have in evidence on the 5th of March -- from the 5th of March is a meeting in Belgrade of the state delegation which was chaired by Professor Markovic, the head of delegation, and attended by Mr. Milutinovic. And from that meeting came a joint statement of the delegation and Mr. Milutinovic, that they're prepared to continue negotiations in Paris, Belgrade, or Pristina, that they're seeking a peaceful resolution with broad autonomy for Kosovo within Serbia and the FRY. The same day Mr. Markovic and President Milutinovic co-signed letters to each one of the foreign ministers of the Contact Group. That's annex 11 to our brief. And what they're reminding -- they're reminding the Contact Group of the situation at Rambouillet. They're asking the Contact Group to ensure that negotiations continue, and they're asking that negotiations continue free of pressure and threats. Now, you recall that on the 23rd of March, before leaving Rambouillet the delegation indicated that more work needed to be done on certain aspects of the political components. And this letter says that the text of Rambouillet has not been agreed, it has not been adopted, and it's far from ready. Now, it's also far from ready and it has not been agreed because the text of Rambouillet at that point includes chapters 2, 5, and 7, and they make reference to that in this letter. And they also remind the Contact Group foreign ministers that they're prepared to negotiate, to continue negotiations, and to negotiate the scope and character of international presence on implementation. And they ask that the campaign which apparently had been brewing at this point to have the Kosovar Albanians sign the agreement before returning to Paris as a fait accompli not take place, and they request that the Contact Group create appropriate conditions for the continuations of talks impartially, without pressure and threat. So Ambassador Petritsch is wrong. On the 8th of March, and this is paragraph 256 of the Prosecutor's brief, the Prosecutor claims that there was a meeting between President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, Ambassador Petritsch, and German Foreign Minister Fischer. Well, that's factually incorrect. There was, indeed, a meeting between Foreign Minister Fischer and Mr. Milosevic. Now, Mr. Fisher was the German foreign minister, and at that time Germany held the Presidency of the EU. That was the meeting. A larger group including Mr. Milutinovic and Ambassador Petritsch waited in the foyer. They were not in that first meeting. Ambassador Petritsch states that while he and Mr. Milutinovic and others were sitting in the waiting room, Mr. Milutinovic would not discuss the Rambouillet agreement with him. Well, why would he?
