The German foreign minister is in talking to the head of state, Mr. Milosevic, about the agreement. The foreign minister by the 8th has received the letter from Mr. Markovic and Mr. Milutinovic asking that Rambouillet not be a fait accompli before going back to Paris, that they understand -- that the Contact Group understands that more work is needed and that they're prepared to continue work. And Ambassador Petritsch says Mr. Milutinovic was critical. He complained to him about chapters 2 and 7. He was complaining about the fact that pressure was being put on the Kosovars to sign before Paris, and Mr. Petritsch says, Well, Mr. Milutinovic called it, the agreement, a fake. Now, remember by this time Ambassador Petritsch knows about the secret side letter. Why didn't he say to Mr. Milutinovic, You know what, maybe you're right; it is all fake; the Americans have gone off on their own and Mrs. Albright has given assurances to the Albanians that in three years they'll have a right to a referendum in Kosovo and independence, which is contrary to the EU, contrary to Russia, and you certainly wouldn't accept it, would you, in Serbia? Now, why didn't he say that? Who's in cahoots with who? That's the problem, Your Honour. And then -- and Ambassador Petritsch comes here and says, Well, Milutinovic took over; Milutinovic killed it. Because they wanted a war? I mean, put aside the preposterous notion that they started a war so they had a window of opportunity. We're not talking about stealing someone's handbag here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, there obviously is a substance in much of what you submit about the way in which these negotiations were conducted, but I'm concerned to be sure that there is evidence to support the criticisms that are made. Now, is it wrong to think that by this time the notion of the back letter had been abandoned? I thought the evidence was that Mrs. Albright had departed from that idea because the EU wouldn't back it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are two -- there are two side letters, all right, and we fully describe this in our brief. The first letter was the 21st of February, and that was a letter from Mrs. Albright to the Kosovar Albanians because she met a day after Thaqi had told the first ministers that it was -- the political agreement is unacceptable. Mr. Surroi asked Mrs. Albright, Can you give us a letter giving us assurances that in three years we can hold a referendum on independence in Kosovo. She did that. She gave them that letter. Mr. Surroi went to Ambassador Petritsch asking if the Europeans, the E U, would do the same thing, give the assurances. The Europeans said no. It was vetoed. The Russians wouldn't agree to it, and the Kosovars were told that evening, the 22nd, that this was not on. Then we get to the 23rd, the last day, and by this time the Serb delegation has said, Further refinement is necessary of the political component; we're ready to discuss the scope and character of international presence for implementation. And that's when we have Chris Hill coming into the room with the Kosovar Albanians, and they draft a letter from the Kosovars to Mrs. Albright, the mirror image of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's what you're talking about, I'm quite aware of it, but that's their statement of their interpretation of the agreement. Is that right? Sorry, I understood you to be saying that the letter from Mrs. Albright was still alive by the time we've reached. Now, tell me what paragraph this is in your brief and it may be clearer there, but if we're -- if you're saying the second letter is the one from the Kosovars, then I quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct, that she's put in her pocket and not told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. I'm well aware of that. I thought you were suggesting there were two letters from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we've -- I've now taken you through Rambouillet, the period between Rambouillet and Paris, and then we're back in Paris. Now, Ambassador Petritsch claims that at this point Mr. Milutinovic has taken over and there's a backtrack to the compromise on the political agreement reached in Rambouillet by the Serbian side, and we say that's not correct. You will recall that Mr. Petritsch acknowledged this, and the letters from the Serbs to the Contact Group says this, that there are -- that further refinement is necessary on the political component. So Exhibit 2D384 is, in fact, the revised document, the one that Professor Markovic says was needed to dovetail the political components of the agreement to be in conformity with the constitutional and legal frameworks of the FRY and Serbia. They did exactly what they were supposed to do. No one can say they're sitting around doing nothing or that they're disrupting things or not wanting to negotiate; in fact, the opposite is quite true. The same day -- and that was on the 15th of March when they arrive in Paris. The same day, Mr. Milutinovic makes a press statement, which is completely consistent with the actions of the delegation in presenting this revised political agreement. He refers to it. He says the document was prepared in Belgrade and makes proposals that do not change the essence of the agreement but improve it. What else happens in Paris? There's three days between the 15th and the 18th of March. Well, again, the delegation requests a face-to-face meeting. They request a work -- this is the Contact Group negotiators. They request a work-plan with an agenda and a work schedule where they can exchange proposals. Professor Markovic told you it was completely ad hoc. There was no guidance, no rules, no guide-lines. The third thing they did, they complained about the fact that the delegation from the Republic of Albania was in Paris. Now, we know the Albanians -- Mr. Petritsch admits it, the Albanians had been fostering the KLA insurgents, terrorists, in Kosovo, and here they are in Paris. And the fourth important point is that the national communities which are members of the delegation had written a letter to the Contact Group asking that the Rambouillet agreement reflect their interests as minorities - that's the Gorani, the Egyptians, and all the others who are living in Kosovo and Metohija - which is completely consistent with what the Contact Group had set out in January by saying respect for all groups including ethnic minorities in Kosovo. In addition to that, you have Professor Markovic who said that Mr. Milutinovic never obstructed the work. He always supported the state delegation. He was always prepared to work for lasting peace and a political solution. And ultimately, ultimately, on the 18th of March, the document is signed by representatives of the Kosovar Albanians, Ambassador Hill and Ambassador Petritsch. Mr. Mayorski won't sign it, the FRY doesn't sign it, and of course, Serbia doesn't sign it. So you have a unilateral signature on a document that we know is politically unacceptable to the Albanians, but for the assurance from Mrs. Albright that they'll have a referendum within Kosovo in three years on independence, which clearly goes against the territorial integrity of the country, clearly goes around the back of the EU, and it's signed by a delegation of Kosovar Albanians that has no standing internationally. It's a non-entity in public international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were these chapters, 2, 5, and 7, ever approved by the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. Another of the cornerstones of -- and, Your Honour, clearly we're not here to have a round table on the finer points of international diplomacy. The point I'm making in defending Mr. Milutinovic is no basis to say that any of this points to criminal intent or criminal conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree. At one stage I asked myself the question whether the sort of misleading that one can detect in this scenario is acceptable in international diplomacy, but that's not a question we have to answer in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, another of the cornerstones of the Prosecution's claim of Mr. Milutinovic's criminal intent and criminal conduct was that after he derailed this process and destroyed it, that he persuaded the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia to reject the Rambouillet agreement, thus creating the window of opportunity to enter into a war with NATO, which would allow ethnic cleansing. Now, there was great fanfare about this in the pre-trial brief and in the 98 bis submission, and there isn't a word of it in the Prosecutor's final brief. I suppose even the Prosecutor wanted to disregard the pernicious lies and fabrications of Ratomir Tanic, who was the only person who even came close to making those claims. Now, the allegations that Mr. Milutinovic did this in the assembly we say is just as preposterous as saying he did those things in 1998 and 1999 in Rambouillet in Paris. Now, Exhibit 1D32 are the minutes of that session of the National Assembly, a public document. It wasn't hard to get one's hands on 1D32. The Prosecution could have got it, as well, and we fully review this in paragraphs 236 to 244 of our brief. On that day, the 23rd of March, the eve of the war, there's a session held at the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia from 10.00 in the morning until 7.00 at night, and three documents are given to the delegates: a report by the state delegation, the -- the report of the Rambouillet and Paris process by the state delegation; the second document is the revised agreement or draft of the 15th of March, 1999, the ones that the state delegation brought back to Paris; and the third document is the Rambouillet agreement which was signed by the Kosovar Albanians, Hill, Petritsch. Now, Mr. Markovic addressed the National Assembly and gave a full account of what happened in Paris, Rambouillet and Paris. It's there to read. He was followed by 26 speakers, speakers from the full spectrum of political life in the Republic of Serbia, including people from new democracy, Mr. Mihajlovic's party, the Serbian Renewal Party, Mr. Draskovic, the same politicians that Mr. Milutinovic had been meeting with or had met with at the end of 1998 to garner support for what the state delegation was doing in Pristina on the 18th and 25th. To a person, there's praise for the state delegation throughout that session. What's denounced is the pressure and blackmail, the threat of NATO bombing, and the support for the KLA. You'll recall that the same National Assembly had sent the state delegation to Paris or to Rambouillet on the 4th of February, 1999, with a clear mandate. But in addition to that, on that same day in 1D32 you'll see that a five-member commission was set up with representatives from the five major political parties, including the opposition, and two decisions were proposed and voted on in the Assembly. The first one is -- was this: The first decision is the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia does not accept the presence of foreign troops in Kosovo and Metohija. Now, the vote on that decision is 191 in favour, no abstentions, no one against; eight did not vote. The second decision on that day is this, and I quote: "The National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia is ready immediately after the signing of a political accord on self-government in Kosovo and Metohija, which is agreed upon and accepted by representatives of all ethnic communities living in Kosovo and Metohija to consider the volume and character of international presence in Kosovo and Metohija in order to implement the agreement reached in this manner." The vote there is 204 in favour, no one against, no abstentions, and one person did not vote. Your Honour, as it happens, as circumstances would have it -- Your Honour, as circumstances would have it, in the days leading up to preparations for these final submissions, world attention has been turned to some exceptional events which are a matter of interest to all of us who work in this international Tribunal and deal with these sorts of problems, and I'm referring to the conflict between Russia and Georgia. As a matter of interest, I make three points. When Russia moved its forces into Georgia, it said it was going in to avert a humanitarian disaster. It said it was going in to bring about regime change. And once installed in Georgia, Russia told Georgia and the rest of the world they can forget about the territorial integrity of Georgia, that the two former autonomous provinces of the USSR, South Ossetia and Abkhazia are no longer part of the territorial -- the territory of Georgia. It's an interesting formula, Your Honour, that formulates in this court. Remember, Prosecution witness John Crosland, the British military attache, told the Court that President Clinton, Ambassador Holbrooke, and Mrs. Albright had decided to bring about regime change in Belgrade and that one of the tools, one of the tools they would use was the KLA, and that the internationals turned a blind eye to KLA activities, and that this was a position that was also present at Rambouillet. Now, yesterday, Your Honour, Judge Nosworthy asked the Prosecutor a question about the October Agreements, and, Your Honour, you were asking whether there would be any legitimate or reasonable expectation as to KLA conduct under the October Agreements. Mr. Hannis says that's a difficult issue. We say it's not. Because in addition to what Mr. Crosland told you, and here we set this out in paragraph 222 of our brief, we know that Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Hill are meeting with the KLA in Junik in June of 1998. The evidence is that the KLA and the US military attache have had relations since the summer of 1998. The KLA political wing and the US state department have relations, and there's also evidence in this case that the KVM was giving logistical support to the KLA. So not only is there acquiescence of what the KLA is doing, we say there's support for it. I believe that's the answer to your question, Your Honour. Preventing a humanitarian disaster. One of the questions the Chamber's had is when was the decision made to bomb the FRY? Well, we know that in the middle of February, Mrs. Albright is stating that if the Serbs -- if the Albanian side sign and the Serbs do not, FRY will be bombed. On the 20th of February, she's reprimanding Thaqi for not being a leader. Now, on the 18th of March, Mr. Merovci, who was part of the delegation, before leaving Paris he's told by Mr. Vedrine and Mr. Cook that bombing will start soon. Members of the Kosovar delegation travelled to Brussels on the 18th of March, and General Clark tells them that bombing will start soon, and what of territorial integrity? Well, we've seen, we've seen the side letter or the assurances that the Kosovar Albanians believed they had from Mrs. Albright. That was never disclosed. And I think we can say that we know what indeed happened in Kosovo just recently with its unilateral declaration of independence, so the territory of FRY was up for grabs. Now, we say it's a matter for the Office of the Prosecutor to decide, it's a matter for the Office of the Prosecutor to decide whose bidding they do; but in the face of overwhelming evidence to the contrary, they're saying that Mr. Milutinovic acted criminally in obstructing, derailing, and destroying the peace process. Unfortunately, they're asking you to rubber stamp the triumph of realpolitik over the law, and you should have none of it based on the evidence Mr. Milutinovic is guilty, and you should acquit him. Let me turn to the Supreme Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me use the opportunity just for the transcript. Page 80, line 18, instead of "again" it should be Mr. Agani; and 89 -- page 89, line 20, instead of vetoed by Security Council, I believe Mr. O'Sullivan, and that is actually the evidence, that it was vetoed by the EU; and 104, 13, I believe Mr. O'Sullivan said territory of FRY was up for grabs and that didn't enter, 104, line 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Zecevic for the corrections and the water break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think it was the territory of the FRY and not territory of Kosovo? No, no, no, I think what you actually -- I'm trying to remember what you actually said, not to correct it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was FRY --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What I meant to say was that the territorial integrity of the FRY was up for grabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me turn to some matters regarding the Supreme Defence Council, and I'm referring to the Prosecutor's brief 137 to 141. Let's be clear. The Supreme Defence Council did not decide on personnel matters, and we say it's time to lay the tired repetition of unsubstantiated allegations to rest. And we say that because the evidence in this case shows the Prosecutor is wrong, and most of the evidence on this matter is, in fact, Prosecution evidence, and I'll show you that. First, Article 136 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it says that: "The president of the FRY appoints, promotes, and dismisses." Then let's look at P984, the Law on the VJ. Article 151 of that law is the implementing legislation which gives effect to Article 136 of the constitution. It says that the president of the FRY, among other things, promotes, appoints, issues decisions on generals' transfer, service status, admissions professional military service, and termination of service. Then let's look at P935, the minutes of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff from the 11th of March, 1999. We refer you to paragraph 74 of our brief. Those minutes reveal that an order was issued by the president of the FRY to the Chief of Staff. The order is issued pursuant to a decision of the military office of the president of the FRY, and the order is concerning the service status of General Perisic. They're asked to deal with it. What do we learn from these minutes of the collegium? We learn that pursuant to Article 136 of the constitution of the FRY, Article 151 of the Law on the VJ, it's the president of the FRY, not the Supreme Defence Council, that is responsible for regulating a general service, and he does this by decree -- yes, the president of the FRY. Now, this is evidence led by the Prosecution, and in our submission that should end the matter, but there's more, the Prosecution evidence, and that's contained in the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council itself. Now, let's look at the minutes of the 24th of November, 1998, P1576. That concerns the appointment of General Ojdanic as the Chief of Staff and the appointment of General Perisic as advisor to the federal government of defence issues until the transformation of the federal Ministry of Defence and the General Staff is completed, at which time General Perisic is destined to become the minister of defence. I ask you to look at page 5 of these minutes, and President Milosevic is recorded as saying this, first in relation to Article 136 of the FRY constitution. He's recorded as saying, Decisions on the appointment of generals are issued by the president of the republic, the federal republic. The practice -- again, President Milosevic: The practice in the work of the Supreme Defence Council was to put many issues on the agenda that the federal government and other organs can decide about. The council's opinion was sought even for matters that are exclusively and constitutionally in the jurisdiction of the president of the republic. He's also recorded as saying he would always in the future, as well, consult members of the Supreme Defence Council, presidents of the member republics about the most important issues pertaining to the army of Yugoslavia. Now, President Djukanovic is recorded as expressing a view, and his view is opposed to replacing General Perisic. He's recorded as saying that he based his opinion on the fact that General Perisic had been the Chief of Staff for a long time and he was good at it. The record shows this was the only reason why he was not in favour of replacing him, Perisic. Mr. Milutinovic had this to say at page 4: President Milutinovic had a different opinion with regard to the issue of replacing the superior officer of the General Staff, although he does not contest what President Djukanovic said. He pointed out that what we need, a Chief of Staff who is an excellent operative. At the international level, General Perisic acted in accordance with political instructions of legitimate organs of this country's political government. That was undoubtedly successful. Nevertheless, he's been holding that post for a long time, and a change should be made, and he added this: "We now have parallel institutions in the General Staff and the Federal Ministry of Defence and doubling of some activities which is evidently uneconomical and expensive." There's a restructuring going on in the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff. The parallel institutions are uneconomical and expensive. Certainly, General Perisic is qualified to advise the federal government and to become the minister of defence. Clearly, Professor -- General Ojdanic, who was one of among many of several candidates mentioned in these minutes, is qualified. He was the deputy Chief of Staff. So these minutes show that on personnel matters that members are consulted, opinions are sought, and views are expressed, and the decision is not within the purview of the Supreme Defence Council. And the reasons that Mr. -- given by Mr. Milutinovic are quite reasonable given the restructuring that's going on in both the General Staff and the Federal Ministry of Defence. And there's more evidence, more Prosecution evidence to show that the Supreme Defence Council did not decide on personnel matters, and that's the session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 25th of December, 1998, P1000. Now, at page 5, right across the middle of the page in bold print, it says: "Report on proposed amendments" -- excuse me. "Report on proposed appointments in the Yugoslav Army submitted for decision to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And then we invite you to look at pages 9 and 10. There, President Djukanovic on page 9 says that this item comes under the heading "information," which means it is only presented for the council's notification but that it is not decided on by the council but by the FRY president. He's recorded as saying other participants could give their opinions, and he needed more extensive information on the candidates to express an opinion. He also says he's heard conflicting information coming from Kosovo concerning the Pristina Corps. Now, at that point President Milosevic says that a mistake has been made and more detailed information should have been provided to Mr. Djukanovic and Mr. Milutinovic, and Mr. -- General Ojdanic provides a file to the two other members of the VSO. Then the next line of the minutes says: "After looking at these documents, President Djukanovic said that that was quite sufficient." Mr. Milutinovic, after looking at the file, says that some reports of alleged lack of discipline and unconstitutional action by the Pristina Corps were usually inflated. Now, the word "inflated" is in quotation marks. Now, wouldn't that suggest that he's quoting from the file he's looking at? Nothing else is in quotation marks. Then there's a final position adopted unanimously, and the position is that in Kosovo and Metohija the Yugoslav Army operated in accordance with the rules of service and the Pristina Corps carried out its tasks very successfully. Now, you've heard the evidence of other VJ officers who've testified, in particular in relation to General Pavkovic's promotion. The OTP witness Mr. Loncar said that General Pavkovic was an excellent -- exceptional, professional, and military leader and that his promotion to the command of the 3rd Army was fully warranted. General Simic, who was deputy commander and chief of the 3rd Army when General Pavkovic was in the Pristina Corps, said he never heard any complaints about the Pristina Corps operating in an illegal manner or outside the chain of command. General Pavkovic received the highest grades on his assessment prepared by his superiors. Another example is General Lazarevic who testified that he did not have any information about General Pavkovic skipping a step in the chain of command in 1998 or 1999. So far I've been presenting you Prosecution evidence by and large. Let me complete this -- these submissions on this matter that the Supreme Defence Council did not promote, and the totality -- before I move on to that, the totality of this evidence shows that there were -- that the allegations of -- that the allegations of irregular or illegal activity were, indeed, unfounded. Finally, I wish to refer to the evidence of a Defence witness, Branko Fezer, who was the deputy head of personnel administration in the VJ, and we referred to him in paragraph 77, and he states that all personnel matters in 1998 and 1999 prior to the war and during the war were made pursuant to order of the president of the FRY, Mr. Milosevic, pursuant to Article 136 of the constitution, and 151 of the Law on the VJ. So but for the evidence of several VJ officers, all this evidence is Prosecution evidence, evidence tendered by the Prosecution and evidence upon which the Prosecutor wants you to rely; and contrary to the allegations, we see that the Supreme Defence Council did not decide on personnel matters. Those are the decisions of the president. There was nothing nefarious about the appointments of General -- or promotions of General Ojdanic, General Perisic. The promotions of Pavkovic and Lazarevic were part of a customary year-end changes in the VJ. I wonder if it might be appropriate to stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I have a little question on this word "consultation." Now, what will be its sweep in context with the constitution here? Because a consultation can -- consultation will normally apply meaningful consultation in the matters of appointment. Otherwise, this power will not be given to the SDC. So what was the scope of this consultation, and I will request you can answer tomorrow. And the second thing is that what the learned Prosecutor has been telling us that in case your client had the knowledge of certain wrongs, why did not he bring these up in the agenda pursuant to Rule 3 or 4 or whatever, 5, of the SDC rules? Now, it will be nice if you could kindly dilate on this to clear such matters, but I won't bother you at this time. You can do it tomorrow. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. We'll adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00 when your submissions will continue.
